speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of urgent and pressing necessity in accordance with the provisions of Standing Order No. 43. This pressing matter concerns the plight of an unprecedented number of Canadians who this year planted unusually large gardens or purchased large quantities of fresh fruits and vegetables from producers with plans to preserve the food for economic relief. These people were confronted with a crucial lack of lids and rings for the wide mouth reusable Mason jars used in homes across Canada for the preserving of fruits and vegetables. As a result, consumers were forced to buy new jars, complete with lids and rings, at considerable expense and a considerable wastage.

subsubtopic: TREATMENT AND REHABILITATION OF ALCOHOLICS
speechtext: What assistance, if any, is (a) now offered (b) planned to aid the provinces in providing services to treat and rehabilitate those afflicted with alcoholism?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: TREATMENT AND REHABILITATION OF ALCOHOLICS
speechtext:
The federal government offers various forms of
1606
November 25, 1974

Order Paper Questions
aid to the provinces in providing services to treat and rehabilitate those afflicted with alcoholism: (a) Through the Non-Medical Use of Drugs Directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the federal government supports preventive, treatment and rehabilitation activities concerned with alcohol abuse. This support is available for research, for funding of demonstration projects, as well as for information and education. Under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal government shares in the costs to the provinces of providing assistance and welfare services to persons afflicted with alcoholism who are in need or likely to become in need if they do not receive such assistance. The Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons Act also provides for federal cost-sharing in provincial programs. Those afflicted with alcoholism may be recognized as disabled persons and may benefit from the services provided by the provinces under this program. Rehabilitation services may include counselling, assessment services of restoration, training and employment placement. In addition, National Welfare Grants offer assistance to public and private welfare agencies for short-term research, demonstration or other kinds of projects designed to test innovative approaches to social welfare problems or to research problem areas of significance in the social welfare field. Finally, the necessary treatment provided to those afflicted with alcoholism by medical practitioners and hospital services are cost-shared by the federal government under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the Medical Care Act. (b) The problems of persons afflicted with alcoholism are receiving on-going consideration. The federal and provincial governments are examining the whole question of rehabilitation in the context of the overall review of Canada's social security system. Services to alcoholics is one area of rehabilitation being studied. Preventive and treatment programs are likewise under study. It is anticipated that the review will be completed by the spring of 1975.

subsubtopic: RATES OF PAY ON A REGIONAL BASIS
speechtext:
1.	On what date was a decision taken to determine rates of pay for various classifications of public servants on a regional basis?
2.	On what dates were zones established within the various regions?
3.	How often are determinations made by the Public Service as to the rates of pay for similar classifications of employees who are gainfully employed outside the Public Service?
4.	In each of the zones and regions which have regional pay rates, what is the rate presently available to a public servant in receipt of regional pay to a similar classification of employee outside the Public Service?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: RATES OF PAY ON A REGIONAL BASIS
speechtext:
1. June 29, 1922. The Civil Service Act of 1918 provided the Governor in Council with authority to exempt positions in whole or in part from the Act and to prescribe regulations where the Civil Service Commission decided that it was not practical nor in the public interest for the act to apply. Order in Council, P.C. 1053 of June 29, 1922, exempted from the Civil Service Act 144 classes of trades, unskilled and semi-skilled labour, and domestic service occupations under this enabling provision. The employees so exempted were paid rates comparable with those prevailing in the locality in which they were employed.
2.	September 27, 1968. Pay zones were defined as such for the first time and established as part of the initial collective agreement for the General Labour and Trades Group which was signed by the Public Service Alliance of Canada and the Treasury Board on September 27, 1968. These pay zones replaced the prevailing rate pay system which had provided rates for more than 350 localities.
3.	The federal government, as employer, primarily utilizes Pay Research Bureau (Public Service Staff Relations Board) and Labour Canada data on rates paid outside the public service in the determination of rates of pay of public service employees. The PRB surveys are conducted periodically at the request of the parties to collective bargaining to meet their needs, and the Labour Canada survey is conducted annually.
4.	It is the policy of the federal government, as employer, to pay rates of pay which are comparable with those paid for similar work performed outside the public service. Through the process of collective bargaining the employer negotiates new public service rates of pay which are comparable to those prevailing in the region or zone at the time of negotiations together with a further pay adjustment for a later date based on expected rate changes for the classification or group.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned last Friday, I was saying that young people who want to go into business have great difficulty in obtaining the necessary loans to realize their projects. That is regrettable since most of them now have a trade and an excellent training, and if they cannot use this knowledge, these talents, the entire Canadian society loses because these young people are not contributing to increase production or provide services. This certainly does not help to reduce inflation as these young people are still consumers even though they are not producers at the same time.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, in view of the present cost of education, this is too much to pay for training the unemployed.
In his speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) talked a great deal about the inflation problem without suggesting any new formulas to solve it. He only repeated well known measures. The government tries such or such a measure, and if this does not work, it recommends starting over again by using the same recipe in case some ingredients were omitted. Here is what the minister said in his speech, and I quote:
We cannot expect to eliminate inflation overnight. It will be a prolonged and tough fight. But we are striving to get the rate of inflation down below the two-digit level next year. It will take a determined effort on the part of all sectors of our society. Self-discipline and a good measure of political courage to get it down to 5 per cent over the next few years.
In another part of his speech, the minister said, and I quote:
We are confronted by the twin problems of inflation and slower growth. They are very closely related, since inflation-if allowed to get out of hand-threatens the continued growth of real income, production and employment.
Really, Mr. Speaker, one would have to be blind or of bad faith not to recognize that our economic system is unsatisfactory and needs reforms.
Those who benefit from the present system, trusts, monopolies and even some politicians, prefer the status quo. But the working classes, low income families and individuals, are this system's victims, therefore they are not delighted with it. It is on behalf of these classes of people that I now speak in this House, to ask Parliament to bring in reforms before it is too late. To cure an illness, one must first of all know its cause. The same holds true for inflation, to cure it, one must first know its major causes.
November 25, 1974

In my opinion, these major causes are: First, interest rates which are too high; second, the increase in debts and the cost of their financing, both in the public and private sectors; third, excessively high tax rates which are eating up progressively larger and larger portions of the salary of human labour.
If there is no change soon in the present policy in respect of the credit which is necessary to finance the public sector, in respect of interests and taxation, our system and economy might very well collapse under the pyramid of our debts and taxes. One needs only look at statistics for confirmation of this statement.
We must remedy this situation. When the Minister of Finance stated that a strong dose of political courage would be necessary, he was right. The government will have to be strong also against the powerful and the monopolies, so that they will no longer destroy through their abuses the gains we expect from social legislation and job-creating programs such as LIP, in which this government certainly did not invest enough money this year, because of the increase in unemployment.
"We shall have to take the bull by the horns", as the Chairman of the Board of directors of the Bank of Montreal said in a speech which appeared in the annual report of this bank for 1973.
Dealing with the inflation problem, he stated that indexation will solve nothing. This is my opinion too. It's a plaster on a wooden leg. The only efficient action, he said, is to take the bull by the horns in grappling with the very essentials of inflation. In another part of this same speech, the minister said the following: "But this question is beyond the interest of each of the social groups, and neither investors nor labour nor any interest group, in spite of the quality of its organization, has the skill and the responsibility to rise to that global understanding. Only the state can. It alone is responsible for that." And he goes on to say: "It's time to make the essential choices. Will our elected representatives understand it?" This is, Mr. Speaker, another banker who speaks like a Social Crediter. Will the Minister of Finance believe this one?
As a solution to the problem of inflation, we Social Crediters are suggesting something. We are sometimes told: "You are always criticizing, but you never suggest any solution!" Today, Mr. Speaker, I will make very concrete suggestions and put them on very solid basis. First, immediate adoption by Parliament of a law guaranteeing each Canadian a minimum income. This income would be added to revenues provided by each person's efforts and would not be part of prices. Second, passage of legislation authorizing old age security pension payments as early as age 60 for those who wish to retire and also for those who are unemployed but also need income to live. Third, a discount on Canadian products sold at retail. I will say more on that later on if possible. Fourth, financing in the public sector using credits from the Bank of Canada and on which carrying charges would not be higher than administration costs.
This new method of financing would put an end to the competition that the Canadian and provincial governments are now providing for the private sector on the money market. This would lower interest rates on the capital necessary to industry in general. It would also
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
contribute to a decrease in production costs and therefore, in prices.
In his 1975-76 budget, the Minister of Finance provides an amount of $3 billion and a half for interest on the public debt. That is exactly one billion more than for 1973-74. If that is not a real cancer gnawing at the vitals of society, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what cancer is? The way things are going, more than 10 per cent of the budget will soon be used just to pay interest on the public debt.
It is not normal that a sovereign government should be forced to finance the country's expenses by kowtowing to those who have the privilege of making money with the country's credit by plucking out of the blue the money they lend government. That is no more and no less than slavery and it is therefore vain to speak of democracy.
A sovereign government must realize that it has the power and the duty to create and monitor the instrument of exchange the people of this country need for their exchanges of products and services.
It may be argued that if that formula were good other countries would have tried it before today. To those people I say that President Lincoln used it successfully in the United States from 1860 to 1864. It is true that he paid with his life the courage and the guts of having dared put money at the service of his fellow man.
Another American by the name of Goldsborough introduced a bill in the U.S. House of Representatives on August 22, 1935. The purpose of that bill was to restore to the American government its supreme role of creating the money necessary for financing the expenditures of the American people and liberating it from the slavery of money comptrollers. I obtained a copy of that bill and had it translated in excellent French. Of course, I do not intend to read the whole thing in this House but I am quite prepared to hand a copy to the Minister of Finance so he can have a look at it and use it in due time.
What was the purpose of that bill? The purpose of that bill was as stated in clause 1, and I quote:
To restore to Congress its constitutional power to issue currency and control its value; to provide a monetary income for the people of the United States with a dollar whose purchasing power will be stable and equitable, adequate at all times to allow people to purchase the goods and services that industries and business services in the United States can provide at full capacity; to abolish the practice of creating bank deposits by private groups on fractional reserves and for other purposes.
Indeed, the purpose of that act is quite clear. Furthermore, the sponsor of that bill suggested that U.S. consumers be given a retail discount to fight, as we are still doing today, inadequate incomes of low income consumers to help them to further benefit from production at prices they can afford. I continue quoting from the same bill: Application of Retail Discount Rate-Upon and following the passing of this act the retail discount rate will be applicable on purchases of goods and services from retailers as described in this act by bona fide consumers, provided such purchases are for the personal use of the consumer or his family and not for resale, exchange or manufacturing.
However, we have been proposing this to Parliament for several years, Mr. Speaker. When we hear that this was never done anywhere else, it is not because nobody thought of it but because, here like elsewhere, we have

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
captive governments, which are unable to take their responsibilities and which are at the service of big business.
In another part, section 305 says, and I quote:
Policy statement: The purpose of this Act is to maintain at all times a rough balance in the national credit account in all banks. The intent of this Act is to control the volume of the means of payment for the goods and services according to the capacity of the entire nation to produce and to consume in an upward standard of living, in order not to have an excessive monetary expansion and consequently an undue progression of prices and so that the present system of issuing currency through private initiative for profit, which causes disastrous inflation and deflation periods does not recur.
Here is an advised legislator, Mr. Speaker. A few weeks ago, the leader of the Social Credit of Canada introduced a bill in this House and he explained its nature. It is a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act so that the latter can give long term loans to the federal government and the provinces for financing the public sector at an interest rate not exceeding the administration expenses. This is why a Liberal member killed the bill, and I am very sorry to see that the government chose a physician for this murder. I had always thought that physicians were rather in favour of life.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if this Parliament has failed up to now to pass a legislation that would straighten up our financial situation so that the money used by Canadians would be created by our government as a sovereign government, it is not because that was not mentioned, but because we have a government that is not free; our Parliament should be free and do something before it is too late.
Some people may say: Under the influence of Social Credit, the value of money is going to drop. There is no Social Credit for the time being, and we still have inflation. Social Credit is not ruling the country, and money has been losing much of its worth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We deal with other countries.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know that. But the hon. member will make his own speech and explain. They say, and I quote:
Inflation has eroded wage increases by 60 per cent.
There is your system! They say that 60 per cent of wage increases are eroded by inflation, which is created by the system the hon. member upholds so vigorously.
An economist quoted in an article of the January 31, 1974 edition of La Presse said, and I quote:
The value of the dollar will go down by 50 per cent within ten years
This is only a partial truth, for we know that the situation will be even worse, considering the present trend of changes.
The former chief of the hon. member knows that. Even though the hon. member comes from the Mercier constituency in Montreal, he has not yet been blessed.
At all events, Mr. Mackenzie King, in 1935, at the time of the great battle to free Canada from US financial domination, uttered some truths that can be verified, but did not act accordingly afterwards. I quote:
[Mr. Lambert (Bellechasse).J
Once a nation loses control over its currency and its credit, it does not matter much who in that nation makes laws. Once in control, money lenders will ruin any country.
We too, in Canada, are in the process of being ruined.
Mr. Speaker, I refer to an authority, the late Pope Piux XI who said-and I wish everyone enslaved by finance people would hear this:
Those who hold the money and have absolute control over it regulate credit and dispense it as they see fit. In so doing, they direct blood to the economic system, which they hold in their hands. Consequently, nobody can breathe without their assent.
This is why we have ill-breathing governments, Mr. Speaker; they have good intentions, but lack the means to fulfill the people's legitimate desires.
I would therefore hope the few suggestions I just made be kept in mind. I repeat that if the Minister of Finance wishes to see it, I will give him a copy of the American bill I just referred to.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as minister responsible for housing through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I welcome many elements in the budget which both directly and indirectly deal with the very real challenges which face us in maintaining the high quality of housing we enjoy in Canada and the availability of housing at prices people can afford at a time of high inflation. In the housing field, inflation manifests itself primarily in very high interest rates as well as in the high cost of building materials and labour.
By continuing to direct his policies toward achieving an even-handed approach to inflation and economic growth, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) assures us of the fundamental stability and strength which makes Canada the envy of virtually all western industrial nations. While no one would suggest that we do not have serious problems, it is evident to everyone that we are coping with these with greater success than others, more particularly than our principal trading partners most of whom have higher rates of inflation and who predict zero or minus growth rates in their real gross national product while ours is projected to grow by some 4 per cent in the coming year.
This basic strength gives hope for 1975. Without it we could not realistically begin to cope with the disturbing drop in housing starts which has plagued us, along with other nations, in the latter part of this year. Over the past six years we have consistently and significantly surpassed the required 200,000 starts per year. By the end of this year we expect to see final figures of 220,000 to 230,000 starts and about 250,000 completions. This would be cause for satisfaction were it not for the fact that these figures reflect an exceptionally high level of starts in the first part of the year, which level declined dramatically to an annual rate of 173,000 starts in October.
Of further concern to me has been the consequence of high interest rates, high construction costs and high ser-viced-lot costs which have made it extremely difficult for Canadians, especially young families, to get their stake in the housing market. While home ownership is presenting problems which we are tackling vigorously, the lack of



November 25, 1974

rental accommodation has reached critical proportions in many cities across Canada. While rents, on the whole, have not increased at nearly the rate of other costs, continuing vacancy rates of less than 2 per cent will put pressure on rents that will be unacceptable to Canadians and their government. Rent controls are not the answer in this market. Indeed, in the provinces where they have been applied they have tended to exacerbate the problem, and I reject controls as a solution or even as a palliative. A major portion of our efforts in 1975 will be directed to the rental field.
The government's over-all approach of increasing supply is one which I shall apply in coping with both home ownership and rental accommodation. It is for this reason that we shall use government resources and taxpayers' dollars to achieve the maximum effect in making it possible for builders and developers to deliver good accommodation to Canadians at high levels and affordable prices. This can only be done if provinces and municipalities accelerate the rate at which they approve building plans. The concern being shown for good planning is welcome. The very real problems of municipalities are well understood. On the other hand, most people acknowledge that administrative delays and, in some cases, prolonged resistance to any reasonable development are major factors in increasing development costs and aggravating problems of supply.
I therefore urge provinces and municipalities to look carefully but urgently at all plans before them, with a view to accelerating the flow of residential building permits in areas of shortage or high cost. This might mean a lot of night and weekend work for planning bodies. However, it is essential in dealing with our current and anticipated situation and should not detract from good planning practices: it concerns just the administration time of such practices.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the specific measures in the budget which will help us reach the minimum target of 200,000 starts which we have set for 1975. The most dramatic is the decrease in sales tax on building materials from 11 per cent to 5 per cent. This, on the average, will reduce the cost of a home by approximately $650. For first-time buyers of new, moderately priced homes we must add the $500 grant which I announced on November 1, making a reduction of $1,150. This is a significant incentive to bring this type of new housing on to the market at prices Canadians can afford and which the housing industry can provide, as proven to us by them, with the Assisted Home Ownership Program.
Demand pressures have relaxed to the point that the marketplace is beginning to work. I want to see homes sell at prices related to their cost, rather than what the traffic will bear. While I am hopeful that this will be the case, I do not intend to leave it to pure chance. For this reason I am implementing a monitoring procedure to make certain that sales tax reductions are passed on to the builders by the suppliers and by the builders to the home'buyers. I have invited representatives of the supply and building industries to meet with me and with my officials in Ottawa to seek their co-operation and to develop and explain procedures which will best achieve the reduction
The Budget-Mr. Danson
in costs and increase in supply which the measure is designed to achieve. My colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), is co-operating fully with me in this effort.
Another factor in the budget is the disallowance of the carrying cost on land until it is brought into use. This should accelerate the supply of land. Combined with the action of some provinces, our federal programs for land assembly and servicing and the reintroduction of Bill C-34 to assist municipalities and provinces in providing sanitary and storm sewer services, plus the co-operation of planning authorities, will help substantially in shaking out a distorted land market that has been under pressures which have added inexcusably and even unconscionably to serviced-lot prices and thus to housing prices.
The registered home ownership savings plan gives considerable incentive to families to save for the down payment on their first home. The sum of $1,000 can be deducted from taxable income each year for up to ten years. This means that if both partners are working they can save up to $2,000 yearly or $20,000 in ten years if that is their priority. Invested at even 8 per cent interest, this would add up to about $14,450 total in ten years for one income earner, or $28,900 for both. It should also add significantly to the flow of investment money which will find its way into the mortgage market which, in turn, will help provide the homes which these couples are saving to buy. Add to this the $1,000 in deductions from interest earnings for all taxpayers, and we have a major infusion of money into the mortgage market.
In addition, I am urging the significantly growing pension funds to allocate a greater proportion of their investment to the residential mortgage market. Mortgage investment corporations being formed under legislation from the last parliament, and the establishment of the Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation, are further incentives for residential mortgage investment. Combined, all of these measures should assure supply of mortgage funds and act as a stabilizing factor on mortgage interest rates.
What I like best of all about the registered home ownership savings plan, Mr. Speaker, is the incentive to savings-an almost forgotten word in these times of almost insatiable demand for all the good things available to us in an abundant society. I have said in the past that every Canadian has a right to good housing and it is my responsibility to see that it is provided. I have also said that every Canadian family has the right to the option of their own home. This measure gives them the means to set their priorities. If a home rates high on their list of priorities, they now have one of the most generous and effective vehicles for achieving this goal. It is now my job to deliver programs to make certain that enough homes are built, at moderate prices, to meet the demand, and also enough rental accommodation for those saving toward ownership as well as those who choose rental rather than ownership.
A growing number of Canadians are seeking rental accommodation, particularly in or near the centres of our major cities. It must be apparent that living in our growing urban centres must be relatively high density and the dream of a single-family dwelling on its own separate lot is only achievable at economic cost, for most, away from the central areas of our cities. The choice for many thus

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Danson
becomes achievable single-family ownership in suburban or smaller communities, town house, condominium type ownership or rental within the city.
The increase in demand for rental accommodation is outstripping supply and investment in multiple-family units, especially apartment buildings, is lagging. In many parts of the country this investment has traditionally come from private investors who have invested in such real estate at its inception or as a secondary market to provide funds for builders to engage in further new construction and as a good investment for themselves. Until tax reform they could write off the depreciation or capital cost allowance against this other income. This tax shelter was withdrawn on the grounds of equity as a result of tax reform. The consequence has been a serious cutback in new construction in some areas. To give impetus to this critical area we are encouraging this investment for those who build multiple-family rental accommodation in 1975 by allowing the application of capital cost allowance against other income.
These measures, combined with substantial funds to be applied to existing programs and the new measures I plan to place before the House in December, will add to the total matrix of policies necessary to increase momentum in the housing industry. There is no single magic, or simplistic, solution: needs vary from family to family, from city to city and from region to region. We do know, however, what has worked well in the current situation and now we can make it work even better. The Assisted Home Ownership Program has brought some 20,000 new homes on to the market at a cost of $450 million in loans. I have allocated a further $50 million in loans and subsidies for increased limited dividend, voluntarily controlled rental accommodation for the last two months of this year-enough for about 2,000 units. CMHC has received applications for over 6,600 units under this plan and is selecting those which give the best value. These programs will be expanded in the coming year in response to the need and the demonstrated interest of the builders.
Because our resources are not unlimited I will be introducing legislation which will make it possible to tap the capital resources of the private mortgage markets to do much the same job. There are still areas where government, through CMHC, will have to be the lender and provide the subsidy to make it possible for low-income families to buy or rent new, moderately priced housing and not spend more than a reasonable proportion of their income whether buying or renting. The family income ceilings for this assistance range up to $8,000 and even $18,000 in high-cost areas.
We want to make it possible for even more people to be helped; but, as we have seen, even over half a billion dollars in federal funds in these two programs alone, assisted home ownership and limited dividend housing, in 1974 is not enough. To untap the major sources of private mortgage funds we intend to bridge the gap in interest rates between the minimum rate at which private lenders can economically lend and the maximum rate at which lower and medium-income Canadians can afford to borrow. This will apply to more areas of Canada and to a broader income range. As the objective is to increase the

supply of new, moderately priced housing, this measure will be specifically directed at this moderate price range of new housing. I will also be proposing legislation to provide warranties to home buyers to protect them from unscrupulous or negligent builders.
Mr. Speaker, the world economic situation is largely beyond our direct control. That which we can affect will be pursued with vigour, responsibility and sensitivity. We are determined that the continuing goal of good housing at affordable prices is achievable for all Canadians even under present difficult circumstances. We intend to continue support to a productive housing industry working toward government objectives.
We are, further, determined to maintain high levels of employment and productivity in this vital segment of our economy which employs 200,000 Canadians directly on site, a further 30,000 off site and two or three times that number who supply the appliances, furniture, rugs, drapes and other furnishings that go into a home. We have done so consistently over the years and have increased our budgets in the life of this government from about $716 million in 1967 to $900 million in 1974. I do not intend to lessen now this momentum in such a critical area of our society and economy. Indeed, the emphasis, resources and impact will be greater still, not only in homes for Canadians but in homes in cities and towns which are increasingly well planned and in an environment in which we can live richly.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, the government has a multipronged and aggressive approach to deal with what otherwise would be an unacceptable housing picture. In the budget there is a reduction in sales tax on building materials to 5 per cent, the elimination of sales tax on construction equipment, the registered home ownership savings plan, the encouragement of private investment in rental accommodation, and other measures to encourage savings and mortgage investments.
The existing programs include a $500 home owner's grant, assisted home ownership for moderate and lower income Canadians, limited dividend rental accommodation, rural and native housing, non-profit housing, cooperative housing, student housing, senior citizens' housing, land assembly programs, land servicing programs, municipal sewer programs, the Neighbourhood Improvement Program, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, programs for innovative housing, the Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation, mortgage investment corporations, and others which complement these. Those are the existing programs.
In the near future we will have the Assisted Home Onwership Program with private sector participation for moderately priced homes, which I just briefly outlined, the limited dividend rental program with private sector participation to increase the leverage for low rental accommodation in Broadview and all the other great places across this country, and new legislation to provide land at economic cost for low-income housing in high land cost areas. This is extremely important in major cities such as Vancouver, Montreal, Toronto and Peterborough. Also, there is the expansion and extension of our municipal sewer system assistance program which is extremely important for municipalities in bringing more housing lots
November 25, 1974

on to the market, and the warranty protection program for home buyers which I have mentioned.
Other measures might be necessary to meet new problems or opportunities as they arise. I urge, Mr. Speaker, that our home building industry and the lending institutions gear up for a year of sustained activity in 1975, a year in which housing starts can well exceed, and comfortably exceed, the minimum 200,000 units if Canada's economy continues to perform as it has and in a way which this budget is designed to sustain. I am not suggesting that it will be easy, but I am saying that every effort of the government will be expended to make it possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to follow the urban affairs minister and to note how pleased he is about all the things that are going on. He says we have a multipronged approach to the housing problem. If you will pardon the terrible pun, I would say it has been devilishly ineffective, whether multipronged or not. I have been reading with great interest the new red book-we used to have Redbook in the United States, another called True Romances, and I would call this one "New Romances"-in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) tells us how good things are. In it he says:
With the benefit of measures in this budget, and with no unforeseen deterioration of the economic environment abroad or unforeseen shocks at home, the Canadian economy is expected to grow at a rate of about 4 per cent in 1975.
It is projected that about a quarter of a million new jobs will be created in 1975, on top of some 870,000 jobs created in Canada in the past two years.
A determined effort will be required by al! sectors of our society to get inflation down over the next few years. We are striving to get the rate below the two-digit level next year.
The Man from Glad could not have been any more soporific than that at a time of great crisis and challenging economic deterioration in this country. It is nothing more than, as a distinguished author said last week, saccharine solutions for a marshmallow world. We are going to have a bad situation in respect of employment. We received information from Statistics Canada the other day. Thanks to information received from one of my colleagues with a constituency of four different names-I refer to the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty)-it is indicated that for Hillsborough it is expected there will be an unemployment rate of 14.7 per cent for this winter. This follows immediately after statistics which show that in one year food costs at home have risen 20 points. This is not only in that province, in that constituency, but in all of Canada there will be a winter of discontent.
The other day we heard that many people in this country, a quarter of them living at the poverty line-and that is not gracious living-are reduced to eating pet food, some of which is highly unwholesome. It is alleged that Marie Antoinette once told the peasants of France that if they did not have bread to eat, they could eat cake. What the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told the Lapalme drivers to eat was neither bread nor cake. However, I do not think pet food is a very good suggestion. We are living today, not in a just society but in a rendezvous with stagflation. That is an outrageous word but it is a much more outrageous condition.
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) confessed the other day that his family was using powdered milk, but months ago he prescribed to old age pensioners a more complete diet than that-a diet of powdered skim milk, peanut butter and day-old bread. What a glorious old age for our senior citizens-stale bread, peanut butter and powdered skim milk! That was the message given to each of them with their old age security pension.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No sugar.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No sugar, and no wine, which was recommended as so nutritive by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). So we have just stale bread at 65 years of age, after a lifetime of service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not stale at a day old.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of the unfortunate developments in a political system wherein one party remains too long in power is that opportunism rises and the capacity to accept a challenge is diminished. One would like to have seen this government which was re-elected with its cherished majority on July 8 come in with a sense of direction, a sense of purpose, grateful that the people of Canada had given it a four-year mandate, instead of coming in with outrageous displays of incompetence or worse. I have heard all the arguments about who is responsible for the loss of 28 million eggs. I am not really concerned about jurisdiction or about who knew and who did not know. In a world of starvation it is an outrage that people should be so casual and blase as to try to explain it away. It is a crime, and nothing short of a crime. I wonder what has happened to the old Calvinist sense of sin.
To suggest there may not be things in the world that require exceptionally urgent action by the Canadian government is the worst kind of myopic nonsense. We are facing very, very grave situations. I am just old enough to have some lingering recollections of the depression. I feel there is a very great danger that we may be heading into the same sort of situation. I have that uneasy feeling of deja vu.
I think sometimes people seem to be cast in familiar roles. In Britain we have Harold Wilson, who might have been a Ramsay Macdonald, suddenly becoming garrulous. In Washington we have a Herbert Hoover without Hoover's fine intellect, great rectitude and proven internationalism. Everywhere there is a directionless sense and directionless people. In Canada we have Mackenzie King-ism; a little more stylish but a recycled laissez faire. This was the way it was viewed in 1929; that things would somehow work out and we would just sit here. We know what happened.
The only time ministers across the floor make any real reference to the international situation is when they invoke it to cover up their domestic blunders. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is famous with his mess; that is a unique thing and he gets special credit for it. The Minister of Finance is especially good at bringing in everything from the weather to the full moon when things go wrong with his calculations.

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie
We experienced a series of disturbances on the international scene. I do not think there is any thoughtful person who is not disquieted by the conference in Bucharest. I was not at all proud of the Canadian role there. The Law of the Sea Conference was a matter of great dissatisfaction. The recent food conference at Rome was a grievous disappointment, and the failure of our own government to deal with the matter forthrightly and fully in this House added nothing to the grim story of what went on when the gathering finally convened.
We have been making mistakes and not even trying to delineate them, much less make recompense for them. Not long ago I went with some colleagues to a part of the world where starvation was not a dictionary word but a daily occurrence. Life there was really precarious. I came back to this chamber and found this government, the same one that is here now, paying for non-production of food in this country. That is another crime, Mr. Speaker. No man, no government, no organization in a world where food has become a constant and vital reality should ever encourage the non-production of foodstuffs. But we did just that. The same people who piloted that bill through the House were quite capable of rationalizing their subsequent failure in other realms by referring to the shortage of food in the world.
Another very significant food product is fish, yet this government has allowed our fisheries to be ravaged and raped with impunity. It is well that the Arctic is not a good fishing ground, because it would be even easier for anyone to go in there and take what they liked.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They fly over it twice a year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they fly over it twice a year and might catch them between seasons. Daily, food is being wasted on our coasts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sovereignty on the instalment plan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Food is thrown away; it is wasted by the ships of other nations. Seemingly, we have no capacity of leadership to bring about correction of these problems. There are problems which should shake the complacency of a government that cares; problems of our own that are grave enough, without trying also to fortify ourselves, as we must, against the buttresses which will come from a deterioration in the international economy. That is as clear as can be, with fluttering currencies, faltering economies and lack of confidence all around. Of course we are heading for tough days, and we have to recognize and fight them in order to sustain our own economy and look after our people. We do not do that by tepid conferences, rotten eggs and the jerks and starts so apparent in our relationship with the United States.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the jerks in government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of my colleagues says it is the jerks in government, but as you know, Mr. Speaker, I am too polite to call them that. I would not call them anything worse than insensitive incompetents; I would not think of calling them jerks.
There have been some fine speeches in this debate, and I commend hon. members who have taken part. I am a great

believer in general debate in which representatives deal with the issues affecting all people. I was much attracted by the excellent address delivered by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) and that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who pointed out something very significant in this budget, namely, that at a time of inflation and because of the way this economy is handled, the people who suffer most are those who can least afford to suffer at all; that is, the poor people. That is the problem. The rich are doing quite well and the government is doing quite well out of inflation. It is not a bad time for those two groups. But it is hard on the middle-class, and unbearable for the poor.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North was dead-on when he pointed out that the taxpayer earning $6,000 will, according to 1975 schedules save $183 and the fellow earning $30,000 will save $622. If I may be scriptural, let me ask for whom, then, should the government show greater concern; for those who most need care, or for those who do not? I submit that a good government cares most for those who most need care. Experts have for years studied our income tax structure, yet for 1975, when the poor will suffer greatly, the taxation system will be regressive and will injure most those who are at the bottom of the scale. The lot of those at the bottom of the income scale, those close to the poverty line, will become worse, day in, day out, as inflation rages. Their difficulties will become more acute until they become unbearable. Yet we are told that the world looks on us as an example of how to deal with people and manage an economy.
I associate myself completely with the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). As my political ambitions are limited, and as my transition from a slowly aging politician to a mature, elder statesman will be accomplished only by the passage of time, I am able to say exactly what I like. As the present crew of our ship of state is more interested in the design of the cabin and the colour of the hull than in the direction in which we are travelling, I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition, who has displayed more knowledge of the economic structure and problems of this country, and more genuine compassion for the plight of our people than anyone else in this House, will reconsider his announced intention to leave the public life of this country.
There were times in ancient Rome when they had to ask people like Cincinnatus to return and help guide the ship of state. As Rome was only about 50 miles long, that journey was not too difficult. But I am wondering if the hon. gentleman should settle in Halifax because I am convinced, fearfully and painfully, that we shall need him in this country. The present crew in charge of the ship has lost control. Although the people of Canada expressed themselves in their vote-and we accept their view and the ancient saying vox populi vox dei-yet I think they will find the next four years exceedingly long, and in the next election we shall not hear very much about minority governments not being as good as majority governments. So I hope that the mover of this motion will still be available to our country in the future because I am sure the need for him will be painfully apparent.
November 25, 1974

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the debate on the budget because in such debates one may talk about the budget and about special difficulties in one's own constituency. This opportunity is especially welcome if one represents a constituency in the north of Ontario. I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on preparing this budget. I am told that his parliamentary secretary had a major role in its preparation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At least we know whom to blame.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The difficulties facing the world are unprecedented. They are a reflection of the instability which exists in the international sphere, which is partly the result of terrific balance of payment difficulties faced especially by oil importing nations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Among those numbers Canada may now be counted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are witnessing the most serious world inflation of 20 years, accompanied by a serious downturn in the economy of North America, especially that of the United States. May I draw attention to what the United States president of the United Auto Workers told a meeting in Canada which he addressed recently. Leonard Woodcock was speaking to 500 delegates from the union's General Motors Corporation council at a meeting in Toronto. The United States economy was under consideration, and Mr. Woodcock said that at least the Canadian budget proposes income tax cuts for individuals but increased corporation taxes. Clearly, the good points of our budget are being recognized at home and abroad.
The budget takes into account threats to our economy posed by inflation, recession and unemployment. The Minister of Finance has chosen to counteract inflation by restraining government spending and by encouraging increased production of goods and services. At the same time, budget measures will increase take-home pay, especially of those in low income brackets. The budget also deals with unemployment. It proposes to increase personal tax cuts in 1975. It will lead to a turnaround in our economy. The present budgetary surplus of $250 million for this year is to become a deficit next year of $1.50 billion. This will present a total budget turnaround of $1.75 billion. The government will incur this deficit because it will implement reductions which were announced first in the May 6 budget. The original 5 per cent proposed tax reduction is to be increased to 8 per cent, the minimum saving is to be increased from $150 to $200 and the maximum to $750.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was no 5 per cent cut.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In addition, personal income taxes will automatically be reduced as a result of the 1971 tax reform bill because the rates are reduced by this bill. As well, indexing provisions will lead to higher deductions for those paying income tax. For instance, a married taxpayer earning $10,000 a year will increase his take-home pay by about $250 per year as a result of the proposed tax cuts. The budget also contains provisions which will bring
The Budget-Mr. Foster
important improvements in the position of senior citizens. There is provision for a deduction of up to $1,000 from a personal pension. Of course, senior citizens and others will be able to claim up to $1,000 derived from interest or dividends, as tax-free income.
This provision is important because I have always thought it unfair that the person who has saved money, bought savings bonds or made other investments should pay tax on the proceeds of that investment. The provision of which I speak will allow a certain portion of such returns-that is, up to $1,000-to be free of tax. This budget moves to remove the inequity that existed in this area. It is also proposed that any deduction which is not claimed by a senior citizen may, if it is advantageous, be claimed by his or her spouse.
I wish to refer to the items in the budget which are designed to stimulate housing starts in this country. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) indicated that the number of units being started this year has dropped back from the record high level of 1973. The minister recently announced a $500 cash grant for each new house of moderate value. In his budget, the Minister of Finance followed this up by an immediate reduction of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials to 5 per cent. It is estimated that this will save $650 on the price of a new house.
The budget also proposed special capital cost allowances on new, multiple-unit residential buildings for rent, which may be claimed against any source of income. This will channel a great deal of new money into the housing industry. The sales tax on construction equipment and materials used in municipal water distribution systems will be eliminated. A new registered home ownership program is in the budget. This will allow young couples to save for a new home, tax free, up to $10,000. It will encourage young people to save for a new home. I am glad these measures are in the budget because they will stimulate housing starts and provide new jobs in a North American economy that has turned downward this year.
However, and even more important in my constituency, these housing starts will increase the demand for forest products, especially lumber. Perhaps no industry in the Algoma district has seen such a dramatic turn around in the past year as the lumber industry. A year ago, prices were at record high levels. In many cases these prices have been cut in half in the short time span of one year. Some one-industry towns, such as Blind River, have had their only industry shut down due to lack of demand and low prices for their products. Several other mills throughout the Algoma area have also had to shut down or curtail their operations.
I believe that these budget items will increase the demand for lumber and building materials. However, at the same time I realize that much of our lumber is sold into United States markets. Their housing starts are down by 50 per cent from last year. Until the U.S. market improves, the industry will not return to a fully healthy state.
Within the past few days the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) announced Local Initiatives

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Foster
Program approvals for this coming winter. They will provide temporary help during this time of seasonally high unemployment, especially this winter when the lumber industry is depressed. Some 24 projects have been approved for the Algoma-Manitoulin area which will create 100 jobs this winter and cost some $320,000. There are also several projects under way in the constituency under the winter capital project fund, worth over three quarters of a million dollars, which will create more jobs this winter. This program will make improvements to community arenas in several communities throughout the constituency. Likewise, it will construct new township and community buildings and medical clinics. Several smaller projects have been approved, such as the improvement of libraries and other buildings. This past weekend I attended the official opening of a new arena at West Bay in my constituency. It was built largely with winter works funds from previous years.
The nearly $1 million dollars in winter works programs will be most beneficial due to the serious turnaround in employment caused by cut-backs in the lumber business. There is a strong feeling throughout the Algoma district that this kind of program, funded by the federal government, is much to be preferred to the payment of welfare and UIC benefits. At the same time, many worth-while community projects are being carried out to provide winter employment which would ultimately have to be paid for by the municipalities whose budgets are already stretched to breaking point.
I would also like to mention the problems facing the beef industry in this country. In some ways the problems are similar to those of the lumber industry, in that prices were at record high levels a year and a half ago, and although the price of top quality, finished cattle is at a reasonable level today, input costs have risen dramatically over this period of time. Items like feed grain for fattening, fuel costs and baler twine have risen in price to levels that remove all profits. However, the real disaster in beef farming is in the cow-calf operation. Most of the beef industry in northern Ontario is cow-calf operation. The two fall sales in the Algoma riding, at Thessalon and Manitoulin, saw a drop in price this year from last year that can only be termed disastrous.
Let me quote from a letter written by the president of the Manitoulin Livestock Cooperative. This letter expresses the deep concern of the board of directors at the depressed prices of feeder cattle and the whole future of the cow-calf farmer. No other business has been forced to take a 30 per cent drop in wages in the past year. The board of directors indicate that unless action is taken many of the cow-calf operators will be forced out of business. The price at the September sale this year was 34 per cent below the 1973 price and 7 per cent below the 1972 price. At the same time, these farmers indicate the following price increases: gasoline up 29 per cent; diesel fuel up 51 per cent; baler twine up 238 per cent; fertilizer up 66 per cent. The letter goes on to indicate that there was a reduction in this one fall sale of returns to the farmers of Manitoulin of $300,000.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced a stabilization program for beef cattle in August of this year. It is difficult to assess the full impact of this pro-

gram, but certainly finished beef cattle prices have been better in Canada than they have in the United States. However, the program seems to have had little effect on calf prices, and this is where the main problem lies today. The minister has indicated that stabilization legislation will be brought forward during this parliament to ensure that beef producers receive adequate prices for their cattle. The problems of beef supplies and prices have been further complicated by the recently announced U.S. quotas on Canadian beef exports. Over the long haul it is desirable for us to have an open border between Canada and the U.S.A., although the present system of quotas imposed by both countries is probably less harmful to Canada.
The problem facing the beef industry must be of very serious concern to parliament and to the government. It will take every bit of our ingenuity and skill to design programs to ensure the long-term stability of this industry. Only with such stability can we ensure the provision of adequate supplies, at reasonable prices, for the consumers of this country.
I want now to refer to the uranium mining industry because of the importance of the mines located at Elliot Lake in the Algoma riding. In the past year or so there has been a great deal of concern expressed by these miners concerning problems of health in the mines, especially silicosis and lung cancer. The problem of silicosis was first raised by Dr. Charles Stewart of the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario, who is responsible for chest x-rays and studies of this nature. It has been indicated that over 120 miners now are receiving Workmen's Compensation Board pensions due to some degree of disability, and others have symptoms of dust affecting their health.
Likewise, a recent paper by Dr. Jan Muller of the Ontario department of health which studied the incidence of lung cancer indicated that 41 people had died from the disease between 1955 and 1972. This figure was obtained from a survey of some 8,500 who had worked in the uranium mines during this period. Dr. Muller's paper indicated that this rate was about three times that which would have been expected in the general population. This is surely a matter of serious concern.
What is not known is whether these health threats are mainly the result of working conditions in the early days of uranium mining in Elliot Lake, when there were many mines in operation with a strong orientation toward production and lower standards of ventilation and less protection from exposure to radioactive substances, or whether there are still conditions in these mines which make them less safe than other mines in the province. To try to discover these facts the Ontario government established two health studies this year and a royal commission concerned with the health and safety of mine workers.
One health study has been directed to the examination of the miners themselves, using x-rays, pulmonary function tests and sputum tests. This study was carried out last spring, but as yet no report has been released. The other study to which I referred is designed to test and assess the mine environment. A test of dust levels would determine the amount of free silica in various parts of the
November 25, 1974

mines. Examination will also be made of the levels of radon gas, which is harmful because it is radioactive. The study will also determine whether there are harmful levels of gases from the diesel equipment used in the mines. Hopefully, it will also be determined whether these three factors have a multiplying harmful effect when all are present.
The royal commission has broad terms of reference to look into matters of safety and health in mines in Ontario, as well as compensation programs for disabled miners. I believe the royal commission's role is most important because it will be able to bring a balanced judgment to these matters and make recommendations should the medical and technical studies not reveal all the details of the difficulties involved, either in the health of the miners or the dangers of the mine environment.
With the results of the studies and the testimony given at the hearings, it will be possible to assess the adequacy of the present system of maintaining a healthy environment in the mines. If it is inadequate, the commission will recommend improvements. At the same time, the commission will make recommendations on the safety of affected miners to continue working, and adequate compensation programs for those who are disabled.
I had the opportunity to attend an international symposium, in September of this year, in Bordeaux, France, on the dangers of radiation in the mining and milling of uranium and thorium. Three representatives from the United Steel Workers of America in Elliot Lake, as well as representatives of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Ontario department of health were in attendance. Great emphasis was placed on the dangers of radon gas as a cause of cancer. Considerable stress was given to the necessity of more frequent testing of the mine environment for this gas to ensure that there is adequate ventilation. It was also stressed that the testing should be done by an independent agency.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is planning to launch an experimental study this winter to develop a testing procedure which will show the cumulative amount of radioactive gases to which miners have been exposed in uranium mines. There is real urgency to see these health matters resolved, Mr. Speaker, both to correct any inadequacy in the mine environment which may be discovered and in the health and compensation programs for affected miners. Equally important in these studies is the need to ensure trust and confidence in mine safety and health programs in both present employees and in new people who will be coming to work in the mines in the future. It is estimated that last year's production of some 4,100 tons of U308 will be increased to 8,000 to 9,000 tons by the early 1980s at the two operating mines of Rio Algom and Denison. The labour force will grow from some 1,500 today to 4,500 in the next ten years. Service industry people will add another 1,200 workers to the Elliot Lake community.
At a recent meeting I attended with officials from the municipality, the province of Ontario and the mining companies, we discussed the question of housing and community services for a township which is expected to grow from a population of 9,000 today to nearly 26,000 which is projected over the next ten years. There can be little doubt
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
about the importance of Elliot Lake to Canada and to the world, a world which is starved of energy and which will be more and more dependent upon uranium as a source of energy in the future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in the debate on the budget and I also congratulate all those who have taken part in it.
Mr. Speaker, the budget makes worthy recommendations but when one speaks of checking inflation, as the government has been doing for so long, and ensuring Canadians economic stability, I have serious doubt that those objectives can be achieved.
Of course some Canadians will benefit from some of the measures proposed by the budget. On the other hand, in view of the present situation, I feel it is important, and we can do so very objectively, not only to blame the government but also to insist that it give much more serious attention to some measures which unfortunately are not contained in the budget.
With regard to what it now proposes, I should like to say how we can have citizens benefit from it directly in some cases. But I shall come back to that later.
I deplore especially the lack of agricultural initiatives. I should have thought, Mr. Speaker, that this government would have given some priority to agriculture in view of its present difficulties and the present situation. I am sure the government and all hon. members now in the House know very well what I am alluding to. They know what the situation is. This is a bad situation, and a disastrous one for the farmers and it could have regrettable consequences in view of the government's inaction in the field of agriculture. The budget speech therefore contains no farming measures, when action should be taken so urgently.
During the last election campaign, our party had committed itself to grant old age security at 60. I do not think I am mistaken in saying that the Prime Minister did what we wished him to do when he suggested to Canadians that he would seriously consider this possibility. I am not saying that the Prime Minister had committed himself to grant old age pensions to people 60 years old. But, in support of our argument, which was valid and interested many people because of the advantages it would provide for Canadians, the Prime Minister had suggested that he was ready to consider this possibility. However, the budget speech contains no mention of the possibility of lowering the eligibility age for old age security from 65 to 64 over a five year period. I believe that this would have been very useful for our society and the Canadian public.
Unfortunately, these omissions are justifiably disappointing for many Canadians and I especially regret them. However, this will not prevent me from asking the minister responsible and the government to reconsider these measures because they are of vital interest for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I had also hoped that special votes would be announced for the establishment of basic recreational facilities in our communities. Some may say that this

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
would go against provincial jurisdictions. I believe it is possible to establish-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is sad to say such things.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) will listen to me, I shall make him a suggestion that he will certainly accept.
I believe it is possible to propose a measure or votes within a policy of tripartite financing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What the hon. member is saying does not make sense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The government has destroyed the provinces.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Bonaventure-IIes-de-la-Madeleine will just listen to me, he will realize that a three-level financing policy could be established in cooperation with municipalities and provinces. The municipality which could share 25 per cent in a leisure-connected project could make an application to the province concerned which, in turn and within the limits of its own planning, would accept or refuse to participate as a province for 25 per cent of the cost, which would entail, following the province's decision, the undertaking of the federal government to share 50 per cent of the expenses.
I feel this three-level policy is financially sound and would not limit provincial jurisdiction in any way. I feel also that the provinces would be eager indeed to participate in such a policy. As the hon. member for Bonaven-ture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine indicated, people will not stop until they have told us that it is illegal. This formula has never been put to the test, and I think that provinces as well as municipalities would be very happy to participate in such three-level financing policy.
I think that we would abide by provincial jurisdictions to the letter if ever the minister responsible suggested to the provinces and municipalities such a policy which would enable the latter to establish basic recreational organizations rather more interesting that any amateur sport policy now existing.
Mr. Speaker, as all other members, I am told that the estimates for the New Horizons Program are inadequate. It is a really fine initiative which I applauded. I was quite pleased to see that the government had introduced such a policy. Unfortunately, many clubs of the golden age in our constituencies have to wait one or two years before obtaining their grant. We know perfectly well that those grants are extremely useful since they allow a group of individuals to meet in the proper premises and keep their zest for life. I urge that supplementary funds be made available to those groups, in order to carry on adequately-an interesting government initiative.
Such is not the case at the present time. I think all hon. members will agree with me that a lot of golden age clubs have to wait too long before they reach their very legitimate objectives.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where will the funds come from?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They will have to come from elsewhere! Mr. Speaker, I should also like to draw the government's
(Mr. La Salle.]
attention to the fact that, in my constituency, the matter of protecting properties situated along the river, particularly in the communities of Lanoraie, Lavaltrie and Saint-Sulpice, has been outstanding for a long time. I made several representations to the Department of Public Works. I always got the same answer. My proposals on behalf of those individuals are all fine, but there are no funds. I think it is time to lift the concern of those riverside residents whose properties are shrinking because of erosion caused by ships or tides. I recently heard that if the Treasury Board agreed to make the necessary funds available, the building of a 15,000 foot protection wall would finally be agreed to. I believe the Department of Public Works could find the necessary funds to carry out that project which would put an end to that unfair situation of those residents. I think requests to that effect were made as early as 1958. Therefore, I have not been the first member of Parliament who made recommendations and representations respecting that most important project.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, some of the budget speech measures are quite commendable. And yet I was wondering how we could apply them so that they would benefit the consumer. Let me take for instance the 12 per cent tax on building materials which will be reduced to 5 per cent. We have learned from past experiences in the area of sweets as well as clothing and footwear that the removal of the 10 per cent tax did not benefit the consumers. For instance, we now pay 22 cents for a chocolate bar that was priced 10 cents. Soft drinks were 15 cents, but today they cost 25 cents. Mothers know very well that the removal of taxes on clothing and footwear did not benefit them too much, except that it was a way fo subsidizing industries and intermediaries. Since the minister lacks control over building materials, I wonder how he will manage to enforce this tax reduction which he thinks will directly help new house owners, that is consumers. I do hope the minister will take the necessary measures in that regard and will create a review board or whatever so that in the end the tax cut will really be passed on to consumers or new house owners. But today, in view of the experiences I mentioned and which we have lived, we must unfortunately question seriously the efficiency of such measures.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as our time is quite limited, I would also like to raise the matter of the extraordinary powers which the government intends to avail itself regarding natural resources within the provinces. In view of the Minister's statement and of Bill C-32 now under consideration it seems that the whole confederative system is questioned and that these extraordinary powers relating to natural resources are defined simply and purely by the word centralization.
This brings us to a confrontation between the provinces and the federal government. Alberta is a perfect example of the marked differences in this country. I understand that Albertans are anxious to keep their provincial rights and jurisdiction. We do recognize at the outset that, con-stitutionnally, such powers belong to the provinces. The interference of the federal government on the basis of those intentions should concern us as MPs, and especially those of us who want to see the provincial rights respected.
November 25, 1974

May I take this opportunity to congratulate our leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for the respect he has shown ever since he has been the head of this party, for the vested interests of the provinces. I also entirely agree with the statements he made and the views he expressed.
Today, it is the province of Alberta which is confronted with the measures this government intends to take. But if we consider the extended powers they contain, when speaking about natural resources and control of our energy resources, we must understand that, as Quebecers, we should also be concerned because, tomorrow, our mines and water resources might be involved.
I am also concerned by Quebec Premier's stubborn silence, for in the next two years, he is likely to want to sell his electricity to the United States.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the federal government will be able to apply restrictions as easily as they did or intend to do. I am also concerned by the silence of little Robert in Quebec and when mentioning little Robert I do not mean the dictionary, but his silence worries me.
As members from Quebec I think we should ask ourselves some questions because I believe it is our responsibility to compel the Quebec premier to publicly tell if he endorses the intentions of the federal government.
When the minister, Mr. St-Pierre was attacking, last week, the encroaching of the federal government I found surprising the muteness of the Quebec premier. It is not the first time that Quebec ministers make representations to the federal government, in the telecommunication or immigration field or another area. Recently, Mr. Cho-quette was claiming a few million dollars as did the Ontario Government. Today, Mr. St-Pierre is attacking the federal government and worries about the extraordinary powers it intends to take. He invites the provinces to get together to fight against interference by Ottawa. Most surprising is that the Bourassa government did not say anything about it yet.
I think that as members from the province of Quebec we should oppose a categorical refusal to these centralizing powers if we are to maintain the objective of national unity that is mentioned at every electoral campaign.
Today, Mr. Speaker, we recognize obvious disparities and not only at the regional level. The ten provinces have differences, different needs and this for different reasons. I think it is normal and it might be more logical to talk about national harmony. It is urgent to reach this national harmony objective as national unity is not for tomorrow. But I think possible to harmonize differences. To recognize that we are different and coordinate measures with the provinces at the federal level and not to centralize, that is the final objective we must aim at.
It is important that members of the House understand what makes us different and what prevents us from attenuating many of our problems. So long as we do not respond to that wish on the part of the provinces to invite the federal government to play the role of a coordinator and not that of a centralizer, we are going towards a failure, and the results will be deplorable.
The Budget-Mr. Daudlin
I for one believe that it is our duty to engage a pitched battle against federal government infringement upon the jurisdictions of the provinces. For us, Progressive Conservatives, it is a decision that we will not be long in announcing. We are going to engage, for the respect of the provinces, precisely for their survival, what we think is a perfectly legitimate battle. In this way, we are assuming our responsibilities.
I hope that the members from Quebec will respond in the same manner to defend the interests of their province.
I congratulate the people from Alberta for eagerly defending their rights to the natural resources of their province.
