And let no one tell me that in the interest of the national good these powers have to be taken away from the provinces. It is unthinkable that a federal-provincial meeting cannot produce interesting results for the whole country's welfare.
I suggest that these meetings are not enough. There is no need for confrontation but we should get together again with the provinces as often as necessary. I believe that negotiations between provinces should be carried out by people who understand the interests of the country and of the province itself.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are mistaken if we believe that these powers should be handed over to the federal government. It is quite an easy thing for the federal government, during wartime for example, to take over those powers which belong to the provinces and then later to refuse to give them back. Today we are being asked to believe that these powers must be taken over and away from the provinces once again in the national interest.
But the national interest would be to have the provinces satisfied in order to bring about the kind of national harmony where differences are being acknowledged and where we are still being asked to participate in the meaningful building of this country.
We do not ask those who are different to build the country with the same tools as we are using. What is important is to build a wonderful country, of course, but with certain differences. This could be acceptable. The differences would be justified, taking individual differences into account.
That is a fact, let us acknowledge it and I think that we would be taking a step towards that much needed harmony but not through centralized powers such as is being recommended in the budget before us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate as the proud representative of the counties and riding of Kent-Essex, the constituents of which collectively decided at the recent election that their voices and opinions should be expressed once again, after some considerable time, from this side of the House.
Kent-Essex is a balanced rural-urban riding located in what must be viewed as probably the most productive and arable agricultural soil in this nation. The north edge of the riding is bounded by the winding Thames on whose shores is located the city of Chatham. That city owes much of its productivity to the auto pact. The residents of Chatham look forward to the continuation of that pact

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Daudlin
and, contrary to much of what I have heard here, they feel it will continue for some considerable time in the future. In addition, Chatham is famous for its food production and owes, as does the town of Leamington with its processing of tomatoes and corn, a great deal to agriculture. I would hasten to indicate, when speaking of Leamington, that it is very widely known as the tomato capital of the world.
Moving to the west and then southerly, we go through a number of small towns and villages such as Tilbury, Cottam and Merlin which have sprung from the rich soil and its food production, the residents of which continue to give strong support to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Many of the constituents of my riding have told me over and over again of the good work the Minister of Agriculture has done. Many of them have said that never has a man so well and so frequently protected, supported and nourished the rights of farmers.
At the southern edge of the riding, bounded by the ever cleaner waters of Lake Erie, exist a number of fishing ports and harbours stretching from Kingsville to Wheatley, each of which proves that in fact the fisheries of this nation do not exist only on the coastline but that we indeed have a substantial fishing industry inland which is doing its part in the production of food for the world. I would be remiss if I did not point out to the House, as well, the acres of greenhouses that exist in the riding, producing tons of cucumbers, lettuce and tomatoes, the latter having justifiably earned for the town of Leamington the designation of being the tomato capital of the world, as I said just a few minutes ago.
I also have the honour to represent the southernmost part of Canada, Pelee Island, just off Point Pelee National Park. Its inhabitants are linked to the mainland by ferry and a recently upgraded airport. It is interesting to note that when I visit Pelee Island in my riding I am substantially further south than the most northerly part of California.
I should now like to speak briefly about a few of the things I have learned since coming to Ottawa. It appeared initially to me that certain superlative adjectives seemed only to belong to members of the opposition. It seems that whenever anything is terrible, whenever anything is cowardly, inconsistent or dishonest, these are adjectives which can only be used by the opposition to describe something which has happened on this side of the House. I have scurried to the dictionary to see whether in fact this is true. I am pleased to be able to announce to the House that these words are totally non-partisan and are not the sole prerogative of the opposition; rather, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, my friends on the opposite side of the House are dealing in excess.
I am pleased to say that I have learned, when I go back to my riding, that my constituents have also discovered this fact. It appears they are not concerned whether in fact the government is cowardly or is guilty of conduct described by the other adjectives I have used. They are content that this government is living up to what it said it would do if it were elected on July 8. I should like to advise the House as well, Mr. Speaker, that it seems to me

the new members who have come to this House are following a respectable, good trend in respect of the speeches they have made here. I think we are attempting-and I claim this for myself since I do not intend to speak for very long-to keep our speeches to a minimum, to be direct in our approach and not to deal in verbiage and excess. In this small way we will get on with the business of government. I think this is a healthy sign and I hope it continues.
I should like now to refer to the amendment on which we will be voting this evening. It reads in part:
-failing to mount a concerted attack on domestic inflation while at the same time proposing measures which contribute to national disunity.
I confess that, faced with such a strong and negative statement, I returned to the budget statement to reread it lest I had somehow failed to appreciate the full significance of what I had heard last Monday evening or had completely misunderstood it. I found, among the budgets other provisions, that people in my riding and the citizens of Canada generally will receive the 5 per cent tax reduction brought down in 1973, and that the minimum tax cut is to be increased to $150 from $100. My mental arithmetic interprets this as an increase of 50 per cent, which I confess I am unable to describe as insignificant or as no effort to curb inflation.
I find, further, that for 1975 the basic income tax reduction is increased from 5 per cent to 8 per cent. This is an increase of 60 per cent, which I also find difficult to describe as an insignificant effort to curb inflation. In addition, I find that by reason of the increase in the minimum income tax cut to $200 and the increase in the maximum cut to $750, federal taxes will be reduced by $615 million in 1975-76 and two-thirds of that amount will be enjoyed by people earning less than $12,000 a year. If that be so-and I cannot but accept that it is-then the people in my riding, and I am sure all Canadians, will not read this provision as being insignificant and will not accept that it does not, in fact, deal very effectively with inflation.
I see, as well, that a wage earner with two children who in 1975 earns $10,000 will increase his take-home pay by $300 as a result of these deductions. While my colleagues on the other side of the House may have difficulty describing $300 as significant, my constituents do not. I can only conclude that if my constituents view all these things of which I have spoken as significant, and I and my colleagues view them as significant, then my colleagues on the other side must be either misguided or misinformed and I invite them to read again the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on Monday last in order to arrive at some new conclusions.
Earlier I spoke of the greenhouses in my riding. I should like to refer to them again in order to emphasize the interest my constituents must, of necessity, have in our energy policies. These greenhouses, of necessity, consume a large amount of natural gas, oil and-not so much now, but of late-coal. The cost of these forms of energy has risen tremendously in the last few years, to the extent that we have now reached a point where the production of lettuce, cucumbers and tomatoes is reaching a marginal position. If, in fact, something is not done to protect the
November 25, 1974

producers against these rapidly rising costs, these products will of necessity be removed from the market. I suggest it would be a disservice to this country if these three crops were removed form the market, because then we would become reliant upon importations from California, Mexico and the southern United States in order to fulfil the demand of the consumers of this country.
I suggest that a possible answer to the problem with which the growers in my area are faced would be, in fact, to allocate a certain portion of the available energy to the production of food; and coupled with the portion of energy which would be allocated to food production, the price would in some manner be stabilized so there would not be a continuing price spiral in this type of food. I suggest that we cannot do without the three crops of which I speak. I think tomatoes, cucumbers and lettuce form a large part of the diet of Canadians and are not items which consumers are prepared to leave out of their diets.
Dealing further with energy and related products, I should also like to refer briefly to fertilizer. The constituents of my riding are concerned about the cost input of fertilizer. I understand that the nitrate fertilizers are increasing in price in a spiral of 100 per cent to 200 per cent. I am glad that the government has announced it is prepared to examine this industry to determine whether the profits are acceptable and, if they are not, to do something about it. I suggest that my constituents, as late as last weekend, are tremendously pleased with the budget as it has been described to them. If nothing else, they see that in fact the government has been honest with them in that it ran an election campaign based on a budget, and since the opening of parliament they have seen brought forward a number of measures which were promised in the election campaign. They see in the budget measures they were told about last May. They see these measures repeated. I suggest that they see not measures of cowardice but, rather, of bravery.
It seems that the amendment to the budget, and the subamendment voted on last week, are examples of what I have come to expect from the opposite side of this House: it is a repetition of what I believe to be formalized in the phrase, used over and over again, "too little, too late." It seems to me it has become much too easy to say this. Perhaps it is viewed as the role of the opposition-though I cannot accept this-to criticize without coming up with any constructive suggestions.
I feel constrained to say that we on this side of the House have learned something and have lived up to our promise to return the budget voted on by the people. With regard to those on the other side of the chamber, it appears they have failed to learn the lessons of July and have come back with a position rejected by the people of Canada. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I speak against the amendment and in favour of the motion. The budget, in all its terms, does in fact deal with the problem of inflation, although perhaps not in the same manner as my friends opposite would have dealt with it. But I am mindful that their proposals were rejected by an even greater voice than ours. I am prepared, therefore, to vote for the motion and against the amendment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) in the House this afternoon. The more speeches I hear from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, the more displeased I become with his policies and those of the government. I have never seen a more startling array of deceptions and disappointment for the people of Canada than are set forth in this budget, Mr. Speaker; and I shall mention only four areas: first, the attitude of the federal government toward the resources of the western provinces is a blatant attempt to shake the bonds of unity within Canada; second, the federal government's charging of the equalization formula concerning tax revenues on resources, without consultation or agreement with the provinces, is shocking; third, the $50 tax allowance to taxpayers, and the attempt by the government to indicate that it is $150 when in fact $100 was in the 1973 budget and $50 in the May, 1974, budget, is a clear deception.
The $50 allowance for 1974 amounts to 96 cents per week for the average wage earner. In a recent statement, John Deutsch, former head of the Economic Council of Canada and now principal of Queen's University, said that the workingman has lost $5.95 a week in purchasing power as a result of inflation. Now the Minister of Finance comes forth with an allowance of 96 cents per week for taxpayers and asks them to apply restraint in future wage demands. That is a disappointment, Mr. Speaker.
The fourth area, and the one to which I shall devote most of my speech, is the wrong and feeble approach of the government to the serious housing problem in Canada. In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance referred to the short-term prospects for construction of new housing and said it threatened, first, to reduce employment; second, to raise production costs; third, to increase housing prices and rents; and, fourth, to reduce the supply of new housing. He said these things would lead to a lower standard of accommodation than Canadians deserve. Mr. Speaker, he is right on all counts. With regard to reduced employment, the 25 per cent reduction in housing starts from 269,000 in 1973 to 173,000 in 1974, means on a seasonally adjusted basis, the loss of nearly 100,000 full-time jobs in the construction industry alone, in addition to thousands of jobs in manufacturing, in the saw-mills and forest operations.
In regard to the statement that it would raise production costs, already inflation has caused building products to soar in price and be in short supply. The minister's prediction of two-figure inflation in 1975 is not an encouraging sign. With regard to increased housing prices and rents, we already have the highest home prices, the highest land prices, the highest mortgage rates and the highest rents ever experienced in Canada, with little or no hope of experiencing any reduction in these areas. The result will be what the minister has predicted, a shortage of housing starts and a lower standard of housing in Canada.
Where has the government failed in the budget with regard to its measures for housing? First, it has failed to take measures to implement the philososphy on housing, namely, that every person is entitled to adequate housing, at reasonable cost. This was the impact of the Hellyer report on housing, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the New Democratic Party, and even the pred-

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert
ecessor of the present minister who said in the early part of this year that adequate housing, at reasonable cost, was the goal of the Liberal government. This afternoon the same philosophy was repeated by this minister.
Mr. Speaker, the minister and the government have decided to treat housing as a commodity from which financial institutions and rich people can gouge the highest possible profits for themselves. In fact, in a speech made at the Inn on the park in Toronto on Wednesday, November 20, before Property Forum '74, the minister set forth his philosophy on housing when he said that financial measures set forth in the budget and other government programs would achieve "more bang for the buck" for builders, developers and entrepreneurs. Mr. Speaker, this is the most crude and cruel statement I have ever heard from any minister of housing. When he talked about "more bang for the buck" he issued an open invitation to speculators, builders, developers and financial institutions to gouge as much profit as they can from land prices, house prices, interest rates and rents.

He does this at the expense of middle and low income people on the pretence that it will give all Canadians the kind of housing they need. The measures set forth in the budget will do exactly what he claims; they will give these people "more bang for the buck". That is the theme of this minister. The government has failed to provide measures to create an increase in housing starts and an increase in land banking of serviced land. It has failed to deal with land speculators and to give direction to financial institutions to set aside part of their portfolios for housing at an interest rate of 6 per cent for middle and low income people. Housing is a social right and financial institutions have a social responsibility to respond to housing problems in this way. None of the measures in the budget will remedy the high cost of land, the high cost of homes, the high cost of interest and the high rents experienced in Canada today.
What has the government done in the budget, Mr. Speaker? First of all, the government reduced the sales tax on building and construction materials to 5 per cent. This afternoon the minister said this would mean a saving of approximately $650 to a home purchaser. I would point out to him what was stated in the Globe and Mail of November 20 by James Purdie:
The reduction of federal sales tax on lumber and building materials will produce almost no benefits for retail purchasers for at least three months, and even then the savings will be small, industry officials warned.
[DOT] <1710)
Howard Perkins, president of the Lumber and Building Materials Association of Ontario, said in an interview that the full sales taxes of 11 per cent on lumber and 12 per cent on construction materials have already been paid on inventories. By the time these stocks are sold-in three to four months-inflation and labour demands at the producing levels will erode the cost savings the federal government said should be passed to consumers ... industry officials said that by the time the tax filters through to house buyers it will represent a saving of only about $450 on a $45,000 house.
There is no guarantee that any tax saving will be passed on to the purchaser. The minister said that he will set up a monitoring process to make sure these savings are passed

on to the purchaser, but that does not persuade me it will happen. I have in mind what happened to sales tax reductions on drugs. The drug companies absorbed the savings themselves and never passed them on to the buyer. I am sure this will happen in the case of building materials' sales tax reductions; the builders and developers will absorb any savings and that will be the end of it.
The minister this afternoon also spoke of the registered home ownership savings plan under which people will be able to deduct up to $1,000 per year, for a maximum of $10,000, of money which is to apply to the purchase of a home and essential furnishings. The minister's statement, that this will be a new source of mortgage money, was incredible. How is this saving by prospective home buyers to become a source of money? What guarantees are there? What assurances has the minister that financial institutions which will handle this money will apply it to housing? There is no guarantee. The minister said that financial institutions will not be compelled to use this money for housing.
How generous is the government being in introducing the registered home ownership savings plan? Suppose a couple that is 25 years old saves $1,000 for ten years and at age 35 is prepared to buy a home. The couple finds that applying $10,000 to the purchase of a $50,000 home, it must take a $40,000 mortgage. Present mortgage interest rates are about 12 per cent. So over 25 years the couple must pay $412.76 per month, and in 25 years $123,828, in order to repay this loan. Probably that is what the minister had in mind when he spoke of people getting more bang for their buck. It will be a bang at whose expense? At the purchaser's expense; at the expense of the working and middle-classes of this country.
If the government adopted NDP policy, moderate and low income people would pay no more than 6 per cent interest and that couple would pay about $82,000 in repaying the same $40,000 mortgage over 25 years. But the minister wants some people to have more bang for their buck, so the couple must repay $123,000 in 25 years. Further, the couple which began paying the mortgage at age 35 will end paying it at age 60. What a great achievement the ministeer has brought down! Is this the way to solve the housing crisis in Canada? The minister also said that certain capital costs on new residential buildings built for rent, begun after budget day but before December 31, 1975, may be claimed against any source of income by building owners. I am positive that when developers and their rich friends read that statement they will laugh all the way to the bank and plan to take an extra month's holiday in Florida or California.
When the big developers in Toronto, such as Greenwin, Cadillac and Markborough, take advantage of this measure they will think Santa Claus has come early this year- Santa Claus being the minister in charge of urban affairs. His idea, apparently, is to give the big developers who control development in the large cities of Canada more bang for their buck.

or deception was perpetrated on the Canadian people, this proposal fits the bill. I remind the minister that the person receiving the grant will need to pay only $123,328 instead of $123,828 over 25 years in repaying a mortgage of $40,000 at 12 per cent. What a saving! We are assuming, of course, that the purchaser can find a house which comes within the price levels set by CMHC. What housing, then, are we talking about? The minister referred to condominium and row housing. Does he want the average married couple to raise children in a condominium? Apparently, the $500 grant is not to apply to co-op housing. Why is the minister refusing to give the $500 grant to purchasers involved in continuing co-op developments? Why will the grant be made available to those buying condominium and row houses and not to those buying co-op housing? I submit that such a grant would help those involved with co-operative housing.

The minister is willing to provide money to builders of residential housing at 8 per cent, but is charging provincial governments 103/s per cent for money applied to rental houses. That shows how the minister thinks. Carrying costs incurred in connection with land awaiting development are not to be chargeable against other income, on the basis that land will be released. CMHC reports clearly indicate that residential land required in the next ten years is controlled by major developers in the large cities of this country. This means that a small number of private companies control most of the land we shall need for future housing. House building will remain concentrated in the hands of a few companies and it is easy to predict that housing supplies will remain tight and land prices will continue to rise. All interest payments, taxes and other related charges will eventually be passed on to the purchaser. Yet the minister says, "I will allow land developers to deduct land carrying charges from income for income tax purposes."
The Minister of Finance expressed fear that short-term measures applied to housing will not reduce unemployment. He is also afraid that house building will decrease in volume and that house prices will increase. He is afraid that the reduced supply of housing will lead to lower housing standards across the country. I suggest that the fears of the Minister of Finance will become fact in 1975. I remind the minister that these fears are being expressed not only by members of the New Democratic Party but by an economist employed by the Toronto-Dominion Bank. Dr. Douglas Peters, vice-president and chief economist for the Toronto-Dominion Bank, said:
The government policy is going to have to be changed to bring on more housing starts than the minister suggested.
Dr. Ralph Sultan, chief economist for the Royal Bank of Canada, said the number of housing starts would not have much of an impact in the short run. It is for these reasons that we in the New Democratic Party are so displeased and disappointed with the measures the Minister of Finance has brought forward, greeted with pleasure and glee by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. He has

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the budget debate I wish to refer to the personal taxation proposals brought forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). For 1974, the May 6 budget measure of increasing the minimum tax credit to $150 was reintroduced. For the $6,000 wage earner who receives an additional $50 under the scheme, the amount is not sufficient to compensate for the loss in purchasing power experienced by the earner in 1974 to date, let alone the further price increases that can be expected in the remaining weeks of the year. In 1975, the minimum tax credit will be raised a further $50 to $200. Again, the price increases expected during 1975 will more than cancel this income gain, resulting in a further loss of real purchasing power to the lower income bracket individual. The maximum tax credit payable will be increased to $750, a gain of $250.
On a $10,000 income, using the minister's example, the $250 increase may, as the minister suggests, cover the food cost increases for a family during 1974, but it will not cover the cost increases in other areas of essential consumer expenditures for 1974, and it will do nothing to halt the erosion of real purchasing power of the earner in this income bracket during 1975. The other two existing, nonbudgetary taxation measures referred to by the minister in his November 18 presentation were the lowering of the tax rate on the first taxable income bracket for 1975 from 12 to 9 per cent, and the indexing measures. It is worth pointing out that these two measures do not raise the real purchasing power of individuals but only partially compensate for the loss in real purchasing power that has already occurred. The minister asks that income earners bear his taxation proposals in mind when making their demands for wage increases. Since the proposals do not even maintain existing real income levels, one can hardly expect dutiful labour restraint in the coming year.
Concerning the finance minister's proposals establishing tax exemptions to encourage savings, as has been said before these measures only lessen the rate at which savings are eroded. The broadening of the $1,000 exemption to include stock market earnings as well as interest income is a useful addition-but an addition to a proposal which is inadequate to start with. Additional, new personal taxation measures proposed by the minister are offered as assistance to those aged 65 and over. The $1,000 exemption from pension income, the indexing of the 65-year old and over basic exemption, and the transfer to spouse capability of the 65 and over exemption are indeed efforts to tax older persons on fixed incomes at less than wage earners. But the fact that, in the minister's example at page 1428 of Hansard, a person could receive up to $8,258 in annual income before paying federal taxes presupposes that a person 65 years old could achieve such an annual income level. No federal taxes for low income pensioners is a step forward: it does not, however, solve the problem of those who have an inadequate income to start with. The reintroduced proposals of May 6, and the new proposals of November 18, regarding personal taxation do not provide much real comfort to the taxpayer. They were necessary, but insufficient. The life of the minister's "tax relief to

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
all" thesis is best shown by the continuing rapid escalation of personal tax revenues.
I would also like to comment on the housing crisis in Canada. It appears highly unlikely and improbable that consumers will benefit from the reduction of the sales tax on building materials to 5 per cent. This measure is specifically designed to provide incentives to builders in an effort to aid the ailing construction industry. Consumers and potential home buyers are naive if they are fooled by the $650 savings figure mentioned by the finance minister in the budget. It should be recognized that this saving, if there is to be one, will be beneficial only to the builder in the long run.
This reduction and the undertone of savings it appears to present will do little but further confuse the construction industry when it is considered in the context of other federal housing policies. This measure is a purely psychological device, intended to soothe the fears of the potential home buyer by creating an atmosphere which gives the illusion that the future is not all that bad. The problem in passing on this saving to the consumer arises from the fact that most builders, due to the recent slowdown in construction activity caused by excessively high interest rates, have abnormally high stocks of inventory on which the sales tax has already been paid. Building industry spokesmen maintain that the government is expecting them to now absorb the loss on these inventory stocks. Industry's mark-up on these building materials is too low at present to allow the construction industry to pay the tab.
Furthermore, the total value of dealer inventory is now estimated at approximately $100 million and will take at least three or four months to deplete. By the time these stocks are depleted, inflation and labour demands, if both persist increasing at present rates will have virtually wiped out any potential savings to the consumer. The best saving hoped for would be approximately 3 per cent on an estimated $15,000 value of building materials per unit. The government appears to ignore the fact that the entire housing and construction problem has been caused by high interest rates, the factor which can be blamed for slackening the demand for building units. Yet there are no measures contained in the budget which would ease this problem. Had the reduction been included in the May budget, perhaps it would have represented some benefit to consumers. However, as the slow season for construction activity approaches, it appears that builders will have little chance to deplete their already taxed stocks.
Furthermore, many secondary industries dependent on housing construction, such as the forestry sector, will continue for the most part to be plagued with unemployment due to the percentage of their activity that is dependent on the U.S. housing market which has declined to an annual rate of less than half the previous year's production.
This government has been accused of many, many things, but it has never been accused of being responsive to the public need except in cases where necessary actions would also meet its political ends. This budget is, of course, another example of this. But since that fact is obvious enough for even members of the government to recognize, I wish to deal primarily with another monetary

matter of which the government has shown a distinct inability to grasp the hard realities. I refer to the decision of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) to build an aircraft overhaul hangar in Winnipeg under the management of CAE Industries Limited of Montreal, to overhaul his department's five Boeing 707s. This is an impractical, short-sighted move necessitated by irresponsible promises and previous poor decisions made by the government.
It is impractical because an operation this size cannot be made viable on the overhaul work needed by five airplanes and some artificial make-work projects dreamed up by the government. The minister admits to having no firm contracts yet from any regional air carriers for their overhaul business and, even if received, there are still not enough planes to make the operation practical on the scale envisaged. It is a short-sighted decision because it ignores and is probably meant to pre-empt the filling of Winnipeg's real need for and right to a proper second Air Canada overhaul base.
I would urge the government to contract out the overhaul work on the Boeing 707s if necessary, stop construction on the makeshift hangar that is proposed, and instead begin now on the thorough planning, designing, construction and training necessary for a facility capable of properly servicing Air Canada's entire fleet, with the accent on the new tooling necessary to service the Boeing 727 aircraft which are now coming into service. These planes will become due for overhaul shortly after the base I propose would be ready for them. By that time they will number close to 30, and with other aircraft from the Air Canada fleet will supply sufficient work for this hangar without taking jobs away from the present base in Dorval.
There are many reasons why this move would be a wise one, both for Air Canada and for the country. Historically, Winnipeg's climate and terrain have made it the most desirable location in Canada for an aerospace industry. In the past a substantial portion of our national airline's maintenance work has been repeatedly promised to the Manitoba capital. Eleven years ago last Friday, on November 22, 1963, the late Lester B. Pearson, then prime minister, told the Commons that the Trans-Canada Airlines maintenance base would remain in operation in Winnipeg for at least ten years. Yet the final decision was made anyway on December 6, 1968, in Prime Minister Trudeau's office to move the base to Dorval. I do not think these facts jive with the Prime Minister's statements at a Winnipeg press conference, on May 23 of this year which suggest to hold Liberal governments blameless for the move.
In the past I have made charges about inefficiency, low morale, labour unrest-and the resulting threat to passenger safety-at the Dorval maintenance base. These and other charges were of course pooh-poohed by the government and by Air Canada, notwithstanding that a number of employees from Dorval backed the claims I made. But I am very gratified to note that, after exhaustive investigation into my charges, the Winnipeg Free Press has published a series of articles on the situation clearly substantiating what I have said. A reporter was sent to Dorval to interview employees and personnel at the base, and his
November 25, 1974

conclusions are very close to what I have been saying for more than a year.
The maintenance base at Dorval is neither more economical nor more efficient than it was in Winnipeg. In fact the opposite is the case, and this cost difference will be multiplied many times when Mirabel International Airport becomes operational in a year's time. With ferrying costs between Dorval and Mirabel likely to amount to as much as $4 million a year while both airports are functioning, the timeliness of the Winnipeg alternative cannot be ignored.
Air Canada at Dorval is overstaffed in some departments, grossly understaffed in others. Basic training in M.O.T. standards, requirements and general procedures is almost non-existent. Tremendous unnecessary costs are being incurred because of duplication, out of date methods and equipment, and low employee production.
Highly-trained workers are being lost every day as they retire early at ages of 55 and even younger. I have talked with a number of these men. They tell me the constant union demands, friction between employees and working conditions have been too much. They have been made so unhappy they have had to quit. Morale at the base is at an incredibly low level. This results not only in low speed and low quality work, but is also driving away skilled, senior employees.
New people cannot be trained overnight, nor can they gain 20 years' experience in a hurry. This is a frightening situation, and one which could have even more severe implications if allowed to continue. Air Canada is the most strike-prone employer in the public sector. Almost all of its unionized employee groups have struck the airline at least once since 1968, some have struck two or three times. It should be noted that there was not a single strike at the overhaul base when it was located in Winnipeg.
Right now there is too much Air Canada maintenance work for one base to handle effectively. This is evidenced by the vastness of the Dorval operation and the huge amounts of overtime pay being handed out there. In addition to Air Canada, work is being done for Nordair, Ward-air and CP Air at the base. In the words of one senior employee, it has become an almost uncontrollable situation in which quality will inevitably be jeopardized.
I quote the words of another employee at the base, speaking about the shift of the base from Winnipeg to Dorval, "The transfer was a monumental blunder resulting in excessive costs beyond our imaginations. Any fair, unbiased comparison of the former Winnipeg operation with the existing Dorval operation would reveal not only that Winnipeg was robbed, but that all Canada is paying a costly penalty."
This senior employee went on to say that at Dorval efficiency was an ignored quality.
Even if the Dorval base was efficient and was not beset by criminally low morale, substandard quality, and severe friction between employees, there would still be many reasons for splitting up the overhaul work. As I have shown, Air Canada has too much overhaul work for its present base, and enough to make two bases viable operations. Air Canada has maintained that a centralized operation is more economical and efficient. This thinking must
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
be questioned. Indeed, it has already been questioned and refuted by experts.
In the Journal of Air Law and Commerce last year, an article by Samuel R. Reid and James W. Mohrfeld concluded that there is no basis for the support of this argument, which holds that profits increase as growth progresses. This study suggests that "a program of periodic and orderly spin-offs of components of the larger airlines appears to be in the best interests of the airlines as well as the public". Throughout the world most airlines have taken this advice and moved to decentralize their operations. But Air Canada, while growing at a rate of 15 per cent a year, and despite the government's supposed regional policies, insists on the opposite. In case anyone thinks that there is perhaps something unique about Air Canada which exempts it from such a rule, let me refer to a confidential transportation study done here in Canada. The McKinley Report was submitted to the government in 1971 recommending that Air Canada operations be decentralized. The opposite has continued to happen.
Facts such as these must make many Canadians wonder not only about the quality of Air Canada management but also about the political factors which have seen the airline moving steadily to centralize huge facets of its operations in Montreal. Even if Air Canada clings to the belief that its maintenance work should be consolidated in one location, it still has no solid argument against a move to Winnipeg. With flight operations being moved to Mirabel, the airline is going into a split situation anyway, considering the immense additional ferrying costs that will be necessary.
The overhaul work could be carried out at Winnipeg International Airport efficiently and quickly. Schedules could be worked out for the new Boeing 727s which would result in no deadheading whatsoever. The economics of the situation insist on this course of action. With the expected saving in ferrying costs, up to $4 million a year, the Winnipeg base would be more than paid for by this saving alone within four years.
Again one must wonder who is playing politics when Air Canada resists this obvious course of action. It is about time that both the government and Air Canada started listening to what the opposition has to say, and started heeding some of the advice given them. With the immediate past record of Air Canada in mind, many Canadians are seriously worried about the decline in services and quality of their national airline. Still others mourn the passing of an airline they were once proud to call theirs.
As one example of reasons for these feelings I refer to the mess at the opening of Toronto's terminal 2, a disaster which senior administrators foresaw but were unable to prevent; the emergence of labour unrest and strikes as a way of life in Air Canada; the deterioration in food, services and reservations; the unnotified cancellations, foul-ups, bumping of passengers, constant busy signals from A.C. phones; and the unobliging, uncaring attitude of many employees who have lost the pride they once had in their jobs and who have apparently given up hope concerning the management of the corporation-and with good reason, Mr. Speaker.

Air Canada recently had a number of obsolete Viscount aircraft overhauled, even though the aircraft has been phased out of service-a program which Mr. Pratte admitted "probably cost us money". Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate with special interest. I have read the budget speech very thoroughly and I am pleased to note that it is progressive and meets present needs.
I wish to join my many colleagues, Mr. Speaker, in congratulating you on your appointment to your new office. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank my constituents for having re-elected me.
Some people think that the present depression experienced by developed countries is only a fortuitous factor and that minimum efforts or a short period of austerity would be sufficient to restore normal conditions. But this is not so. The prosperity of developed countries mostly rests upon the processing of raw materials bought from developing countries often at ridiculously low prices. These same countries are just beginning to realize that they were being exploited and that on top of it all their raw materials, being their only resources, are not inexhaustible. People tend easily to believe that the oil crisis

November 25, 1974

was brought about by the war in the Middle East, and is the only cause of inflation that we experience. Really, the increase in oil prices is only one of the causes of inflation at this time and we should keep in mind that the costs of raw materials had already been rising since the middle of 1972.
The situation will never be as it was before and it becomes clearer every day that we are living in a system based essentially on lack of foresight and wastage. Inflation as we know it now should incite us not to regret the situation that was before but rather to review our way of life.
The United States are a good example of this. It is no use having a gross national product increase year in and year out, if this growth is due to the manufacturing of absolutely useless products that, in addition, do not bring any deep satisfaction to individuals who contribute, finally, to deteriorate the environment. What is the use of sending a few men on the moon if, on this earth, millions of people live in inhuman cities where it is impossible to take a walk in the street at night without taking the risk of being assassinated.
Canada is fortunate in having abundant resources, with an environment that is generally not deteriorated beyond repair. We must therefore take this opportunity to avoid errors made elsewhere, and to create our own lifestyle where individuals may thrive. We should emphasize the improvement public equipment, because the percentage of our resources used to improve our public services is definitely inadequate, as compared to the consumption of often unnecessary products.
For this reason, we must contain excessive individualism to the extent it goes contrary to common interest, and use our limited resources in a more logical way. The liberal government has been working in that direction in a number of important areas, namely, urban development, housing, public transit and pollution control.
In the area of urban development in particular, the federal government has made considerable efforts in the National capital area to show other cities in the country that an urban centre can very well expand while keeping human prospective. May I refer to the preservation of historical buildings, such as Academie-de-la-Salle which, once renovated, will be occupied by Urban Affairs offices. Negotiations are also under way to preserve the Ottawa Archdiocese building. These are but a few examples of well planned modernization.
Another urban planning measure also deserving mention is Rideau Square, which is designed to renovate, preserve and animate a commercial and tourist centre right in the downtown area of our National Capital, in keeping with the wishes of the communities involved.
But as often happens, even the best of things generate new problems. Indeed, fast population growth, high family formation rate, and the attraction of a pleasant National Capital all helped increase housing demand. In the Ottawa-Vanier constituency in particular, catching up had to be done in the area of social housing.
The Budget-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier
In order to correct this social situation, the federal government has allocated important sums for the construction of new housing. The accent is being put on so-called social housing, as I said before, to provide housing for senior citizens and middle-income earners. Through provincial agencies, many of these buildings were built in my riding over the last three years.
It follows from that experience that the funds loaned by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provincial housing authorities must be under a much stricter control than it has been the case up to date. The federal government at present has no direct qualitative or quantitative control over those buildings. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation lends up to 90 per cent of the cost of those buildings. Since the federal government has no control whatsoever over the planning and management of those buildings, it is not sure that the loans granted always produce the planned benefits.
I suggest that in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier, the situation in this respect is alarming. The Ontario Housing Corporation has apparently become an aid agency for speculators rather than the population. It seems impossible to me that a provincial corporation has accepted to pay prices as high as those which were paid for land located in my riding or elsewhere without there being any negligence and maybe even collusion involved between certain speculators and certain civil servants.
Such assumptions are most certainly in order, Mr. Speaker, if we take into account the proceedings brought against certain officials of this agency in Ontario.
I would now like to quote an example which I am very familiar with. In May of 1971, when I was trustee for the Ottawa School Board, there were discussions for the purchase of one and a half acre of land belonging to the Ottawa Episcopal Corporation and located on Donald street. The asking price for that land was then $35,000 approximately. In September of 1971, the planning committee of the School Board, having examined the question, recommended the purchase of this land and started the necessary negotiations through their legal counsel. Needless to say, I was quite surprised when I learned that, in the meantime, one of our own trustees had taken out an option on that same land and finally bought it through his company for $105,000. A little later, on March 22, 1973, he sold in to the Ontario Housing Corporation for the sum of $273,000, therefore turning, in less than nine months, a profit of 155 per cent or $168,000. It seems to me that provincial or other organizations entitled to it should use the tool that is expropriation to prevent that kind of profiteering. Since that time the province of Ontario legislated against speculators by passing an act entitled the Land Speculation Tax Act. Needless to recall that that act does not apply to sales to government agencies. I also suspect, Mr. Speaker, that several other transactions of this kind took place in my riding. However, I leave it up to the provincial MLA to raise that whole question at the Ontario legislature and determine whether those allegations have any base.
I think the example I just quoted proves that the province of Ontario and its agency-the Ontario Housing Corporation-are thwarting all the efforts of the federal government in the field of social housing in Ottawa, and in

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier part in my riding. But, as always, it is the people who will pay for it and the community who will be impoverished because that profiteering increases the price of all land in the city, in the riding where I live. How is it that for land of equal value the municipality of Vanier, for example, pays $5 a square foot when the Ontario Housing Corporation pays two and three times that price for nearby land?
Such action on the part of the provincial corporation contributes to increased prices for land. But speculation is only one cause of the housing crisis. Provincial and municipal governments, in addition to stopping real estate speculation, will have to try and discover new solutions to that problem. They will have, on a much larger scale than now, to create land banks that they will resell themselves. In proceeding in that way, using their powers of expropriation, governments will pay the fair market value for land and sell them in turn at a reasonable price, because there will not have been any speculators to make exaggerated profits between the time of the purchase and that of the sale. It will be necessary to make experiences in the area of city planning. It may also be necessary to generalize the creation of satellite towns situated some distance from existing major urban centers. Let me remind the House that such a satellite town with a projected population of 100,000 will be created in Carlsbad Springs, on the outskirts of Ottawa.
As far as the present urban-oriented architecture is concerned, it is completely outdated and will not allow an increase in population density without a possible deterioration of the quality of life. It is in fact as an incentive to innovate in this area that the federal government has invested $100 million in a program entitled "Urban Demonstration Program".
I pointed out that the opposition, because of its usual lack of imagination, criticized this program as soon as it was proposed. The members on the other side of the House probably have not the necessary intelligence to realize its full significance. However, in the meantime, because it felt it to be an urgent matter, in the budget speech, the federal government presented or adopted various measures which might help and bring a fast and immediate improvement in the housing field. First, the carrying costs on land awaiting development should not be charged against other income but be taken into account only as land is sold. I suggest that this measure should assist in bringing land for housing onto the market more quickly. Then the sales tax on building materials is reduced and the sales tax on materials purchased by local governments for use in the construction of water distribution system is abolished. Moreover, to help young people accumulate the savings required for buying a home, a new savings plan is being established: a registered home ownership plan. Finally, the main credit institutions are invited not to confine high ratio loans to middle- and lower-priced housing.
As for public transport, in the budget the government shows undoubtedly that they are doing what they have pledged themselves to do in the last election campaign, by proposing the removal of the sales tax on any transportation equipment, which includes railway cars heavy trucks, buses and commercial planes. The removal of that tax will deprive the federal government of about $100 million of income. As for the protection of environment, Mr. Speaker,

the government has reintroduced for two more years the fast paying off of the equipment used to fight pollution, a measure which was to come to an end within the current year.
But while the government is taking care of the material comfort of the people, it cannot be said that it is neglecting intellectual matters. In that field, the government has shown interest in some undertakings which, if they succeed, will contribute a lot to the development of a typically Canadian culture. May I be allowed to mention more specifically the case of the CBC which has now undertaken to set up an organization to be entrusted with the distribution, for educational purposes, of audio and visual tapings of the broadcasts of the corporation. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
