AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at eight p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam' Speaker, I should like to continue the speech I was delivering before dinner by reminding hon. members that I was dealing with all the audio-visual material and the huge library that belong to the CBC and that should be made available to the public at large, I think, since after all, it is the Canadian taxpayers who paid the broadcasts that may be useful in education or in other fields.
It seems to me the National Film Board could very well take the responsibility of distributing that audio-visual material. Recordings are often a source of information of an unparalleled richness and they could be used for educational purposes throughout this country instead of being left to deteriorate in warehouses as happens at the present time.
An organization such as this one would be especially useful to all francophone minorities outside Quebec for which it is extremely difficult to obtain French culture instruments.
Besides it is to help the French-speaking minorities outside Quebec and even the province of Quebec in particular that the federal government concerns itself with the problem related to textbooks. As a matter of fact, a conference convened by the Secretary of State is being held in Ottawa today to examine all that question. It is almost impossible for the francophone minorities to obtain those textbooks they so greatly need. Purely Canadian textbooks written in French are almost non-existent, and the people concerned have to resort either to textbooks imported from France, which do not reflect the Canadian situation, or to English textbooks.
Madam Speaker, I should like also to deal with a very important question, namely bilingualism.
I shall not deal with the programs now under way in the public service, nor with the policy of institutional bilingualism, but rather with a linguistic centre, in the private
November 25, 1974

sector, which would be located in the national capital of our country. At the present time, 35 per cent of all workers in the national capital area are public servants, and 65 per cent are employed in other sectors.
That private linguistic centre would allow more than two-thirds of the workers in the national capital area to learn a second language and perfect their knowledge of their mother tongue.
I am talking about setting up, in the national capital, a service considered essential by several people, if ever we are to achieve the objective of a Canadian national capital that truly reflects the bilingual character of Canada. That centre would be supported by the expertise of the Language Training Centre of the public service and Algonquin College, and would be designed according to a centralized administrative formula with a qualified teaching staff, grouped in teams; they would, in fact, belong to an academic centre, and be composed of mobile teams that would go to the private sector to dispense their instruction.
The National Capital Commission now has a budget of $250,000 earmarked for the development of bilingualism in the national capital. Numerous public, municipal, and regional organizations as well as several industries and businesses are asking for financial assistance from the NCC to enable them to adopt bilingualism in fact.
In the public sector, at the municipal and regional levels, the need for bilingualism is felt very strongly, whether it be in the police forces of Hull or Ottawa, in the fire departments, in the hospitals and in other fields of public administration generally. I think that it would be possible to establish that language centre for public and private affairs with the co-operation of the National Capital Commission, the provinces concerned and the private sector.
My discussions with several organizations have shown the interest and merits of such an undertaking. I hope, Madam Speaker, that Algonquin College, the National Capital Commission, the Quebec and Ontario governments will take an active interest in the matter.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I wish to say that this budget, which can be qualified as expansionist, helps to promote economic activity in Canada.
Reducing taxes, while increasing the purchasing power of Canadians, it copes adequately with the threats of depression by which we are all concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all let me say that I am very pleased to be participating in this debate with you in the chair. At the risk of being accused of being a male chauvinist I will say that you bring to the chair a charm and dignity which is all too apparent tonight-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and which we always admire in you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But you are still not going to get more than 20 minutes!
The Budget-Mr. McGrath

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course I have a certain advantage since I happen to be closer to the chair than most members. I am sure, however, that your qualities are apparent to all.
Just one day after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) brought down the budget, Statistics Canada released the regional cities index. This is a breakdown of the consumer price index according to the principal cities in the country. It showed some very interesting things. For instance, my own city of St. John's, Newfoundland, had by far the highest over-all increase in the cost of living of any city in the country, although Winnipeg and Edmonton were not too far behind.
Of particular significance was the fact that the food component of the index for the month of October in St. John's showed a startling 3.8 per cent increase. That represented a 20.8 per cent over-all increase in one year.
It was also interesting to note that the figures showed that, while St. John's, Newfoundland had by far the highest rate of increase in the cost of food, Ottawa had by far the lowest increase in the cost of food, .4 per cent. I say that is significant because Ottawa usually has one of the highest rates of increase of any city that is surveyed.
I believe the reason for the change was due in no small part to the fact that the Food Prices Review Board selected Ottawa as the site of a pilot study. It surveyed food prices on a comparative basis in the city of Ottawa, in all of the major supermarket chains operating in the Ottawa-Hull area. The results of the surveys were made public and, as a consequence, there followed real competition between the various supermarket chains to lower food prices.
I raised this question at the time and I ask it again tonight; when can we expect similar surveys in other cities in Canada? After all, the Food Prices Review Board is a national board with national responsibilities. One of the interesting things to come out of the survey was the fact that food prices in Ottawa did go down as a consequence of publishing the findings of the survey.
Another interesting thing to come out of the survey was that supermarkets in the lower income areas, where consumers are virtually locked into dealing with a particular supermarket in their neighbourhoods because of their not being as mobile as consumers in the other areas, perhaps through lack of a family car, charged higher prices for food. I am told the same thing applies in Montreal. I certainly hope that aspect of the study will receive more attention from the Food Prices Review Board, and also from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The increase in food prices in the city of St. John's by 3.8 per cent in the month of October compares with the national monthly increase of 1.4 per cent. This obviously means that food prices are rising at a more striking and rapid rate in St. John's than in other cities of the country. We have also a substantially higher rate of increase in unemployment in my city. It too is growing there at a faster rate than in other cities.
It is easy to deal in statistics, Madam Speaker, but I believe that they tell only part of the story. In order to translate these statistics into real practical terms I did a survey of my own. I picked out a national supermarket

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
chain in the city of Ottawa and a similar chain store in the city of St. John's just at random, and I picked out a number of essential food items.
Here is what I found: in St. John's, one dozen Grade A eggs, 99 cents-in Ottawa, 75 cents; in St. John's, a quart of milk, 57 cents-in Ottawa, 49 cents; a 24-ounce loaf of white broad in St. John's, 47 cents-Ottawa, 36 cents; 10 pounds of potatoes, in St. John's, 98 cents-in Ottawa, 69 cents, hamburger in St. John's, 98 cents a pound-in Ottawa, 75 cents a pound; ground chuck, in St. John's $1.38 a pound-the same in Ottawa, 95 cents a pound.
How could there be such a differential, Madam Speaker? Obviously transportation is a factor, but is it that much of a factor? I doubt it. Earlier this month the Food Prices Review Board released a special study of food prices in the province of Newfoundland compared with food prices prevailing elsewhere in Canada. The board thought this disparity was great enough to warrant a special study, and that in itself is significant.
While the findings of the board were by no means conclusive, it did make some very worth-while recommendations to both levels of government. These recommendations are significant. First of all, Newfoundland has to import most of what it consumes from the mainland, so transportation is a significant factor. And if the board's recommendations were accepted, the distribution system within the province would be improved.
I hope that the study and its recommendations receive immediate and serious consideration from both the federal and provincial governments.
One area where the federal government could take immediate and unilateral action is in regard to the recommendation that the consumer subsidy on powdered milk also be applied to evaporated milk. The per capita consumption of evaporated milk in Newfoundland is considerably higher than the per capita consumption of powdered skim milk in the rest of Canada. I have already asked the government to take immediate action on this recommendation in the report.
There is no doubt in my mind that there must be fundamental changes in business practices in the province. The board has telling and meaningful things to say on this aspect, and I hope the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and his provincial counterpart will take into account the board's conclusions and recommendations.
In October another study was undertaken on Newfoundland transportation. That study was commissioned by the Canadian Transport Commission into all phases of ground transport in Newfoundland. That study, which was prepared by professional consultants, is in 11 volumes. Since the commission has invited the public to make submissions on the report no later than the end of January, 1975, I will reserve my comments, except to say that I hope the study will receive the immediate consideration of the government, so that when the period for public submission has ended we can expect some direction from the government as to what course it intends to follow in implementing the principles, conclusions and recommendations of the report. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion

(Mr. Jamieson) carries great responsibilities in this field, by virtue of the responsibilities of his portfolio, and because he is the province's representative in the government of Canada. As the months go on we shall watch the minister's reactions to the public submissions and to the final disposition of the study by the government.
Transportation is the key to closing the gap between food prices in Newfoundland and food prices in the rest of the country. A substantial proportion of what we consume must be brought in from the mainland and distributed over an area covering 156,000 square miles. Therefore an adequate transport system is both vital and essential. It is not enough for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to say in this House that we are spending $50 million on the gulf service. I submit that we are not getting full value for that money because of the archaic thinking which the Department of Transport has adhered to in matters of transportation affecting Newfoundland, and because of the archaic thinking of the CNR. We live in a day of modern transportation technology, when modern developments have made possible modern transport systems, yet we still operate in the steamship era in providing service to Newfoundland.
Food prices in Canada accounted for over half of the increase in the consumer price index during the past two years. That is an astounding fact. Food prices in the past 24 months in Canada have risen by almost 40 per cent, leaving low income earners and those on fixed incomes to shoulder a particularly heavy burden. Because of high unemployment and a per capita income that lags 35 per cent below the national average, Newfoundland has been harder hit by this wave of inflation than the rest of the country. This places a particularly unfair burden on "the people of my province. For that reason, although we look to the government of Canada for immediate relief-I am sorry to say that such relief is not evident in the measures proposed in the budget-we look forward to realizing the potential of our own natural resources over the long term. That is why I regret particularly the decision of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to tax resource development in Canada, and I emphasize the decision to tax oil and gas.
This brings me to my next point. Newfoundland has just completed its first 25 years as a province of Canada. We became part of Canada 25 years ago after a referendum in which less than 52 per cent of the people of Newfoundland voted to confederate with Canada. I do not think it is unreasonable to say that if we had known, when Newfoundland was about to enter Confederation, that one day the government of Canada would unilaterally and arbitrarily abdicate its position vis-a-vis the British North America Act, if we had known that the ownership of natural resources would be called into question, that fact alone, I submit, would have been enough to keep us, the people of Newfoundland, out of Confederation.
The people of Newfoundland would never have voted to confederate with Canada if they had known in 1949 that they would lose their right to exploit their own natural resources. Let me point out that we entered confederation with Canada as a full-fledged dominion, with full sovereignty over our resources. We are not a big province. Our population is small and we are represented in this House
November 25, 1974

by only seven seats. The province contains only a small percentage of the population of Canada, but we will fight any attempt by the government to take over control of our resources or to change in any way the pact of Confederation. I support what my leader said in this House. And I support the position adopted by the Premier of Alberta. I can sum up our position in no finer way than by repeating what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said, "The provinces of Canada may not be sovereign states, but neither are they colonies".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a newly elected member I rise to speak in this House, over which Your Honour presides with such fairness and competence, feeling very much aware of the responsibilities of an elected representative taking part in this debate. No matter how long or how deeply one has considered beforehand, the actual moment of speaking in this House, following the mandate solemnly given in a democratic election, is one that makes one think anew of one's commitment to the democratic process and of one's duty to listen to constituents, to evaluate their needs and expectations, and to strive to have these reflected in legislation.
The riding which I have the honour to represent is an urban one with a high concentration of new Canadians. It is a riding where many people work hard, and struggle to buy homes and educate their children on modest incomes. The 1971 census figures showed the average income of heads of families as $6,347; the average family income was $8,658. In 1971 only 7.6 per cent of families had incomes of over $15,000.
The measures announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to maintain a good level of production and employment are welcomed by my constituents who are particularly vulnerable in times of low employment. The measures to stimulate housing construction are of special interest in a riding where 10.1 per cent of those in the labour force are employed in the construction industry. The more prosperous families in Trinity are very socially aware and will, I know, support the measures taken to increase the purchasing power of those on low incomes.
According to the 1971 census figures, 8.6 per cent of Trinity's population was over the age of 65 years; of these, 61 per cent were women. The recent amendments to the Canada Pension Plan and the reductions in personal income tax announced in the budget ease the current difficulties of senior citizens but, Madam Speaker, many of the retired women contributed during their working years to private pension plans which have not served them well; still others worked for many years in jobs where they were excluded from all fringe benefits.
Women who are employed in the service, trade and manufacturing industries are often doubly disadvantaged by low wages, which allow little or no margin for saving, and by discriminatory pension plans. Minimum wage legislation appears to have narrowed the male-female wage differential in low-wage occupations, but differentials still exist, particularly in non-unionized establishments. A recent Ontario study estimated the average differential as high as 22 percentage points.
The Budget-Miss Nicholson
In May, 1972, legislation was introduced in this House to amend the Canada Labour Code to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex and marital status. That bill, which did not receive third reading before dissolution of the twenty-eighth parliament, contained a limitation clause excluding pensions and life insurance plans from the amendments.
The province of Ontario in 1971 enacted a human rights code which prohibited discrimination in employment on the grounds of sex or marital status, but the section on fringe benefits has not yet been proclaimed. Since fringe benefits are generally considered part of pay, women are increasingly asking why a country and a province which advocate equal pay can at the same time tolerate inequality of fringe benefits.
Among the many discriminatory practices to be found in employees' group insurance plans are, first, eligibility requirements. Length of service for eligibility varies for men and women, for example, five years service or 25 years of age for women, before entry into the plan. Vesting of the plan, continuous service stipulation, is sometimes longer for women than for men.
Second, take the case of death benefits to spouse. Most plans provide for reduced benefits to the spouse of a deceased male contributor, but nothing for the spouse of a deceased female contributor. There are many variants relating to dependent children of a deceased contributor. For example, the children of a deceased woman contributor must prove a situation of hardship and/or receive lesser amounts that those provided for the dependent children of a man contributor. Most plans have fewer joint and survivorship options available for women contributors.
Third, many firms have an earlier compulsory retirement age for women resulting in lower contributions from both employee and management and, therefore, lower pension benefits. This practice is now changing. However, there are still almost a quarter, some 23.2 per cent, of those women who are now enrolled in pension plans who are required to retire at an earlier age than men under the same plans. When the earlier retirement age is combined with the delayed entry I mentioned earlier, a woman's pension is doubly depressed.
Fourth, there are amounts of life insurance. Many plans offer lower amounts of life insurance coverage to women. The group life insurance plan of one Crown corporation provides single women with exactly half the amount of insurance protection which a single man buys for the same premium.
Fifth, there is the example of health insurance plans. Management generally contributes to these plans but does not allow the married female employee to participate unless legally separated, divorced or widowed. In situations where the wife is the permanent worker, the husband must pay the premiums on a private basis and the couple lose the management contribution normally extended to married men.
Sixth, look at part-time employees. Some firms have no plans-pensions, medical, life, disability-for a part-time and/or temporary workers. Since many women are in this category because of family responsibilities they are par-
1646

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Miss Nicholson
ticularly discriminated against in loss of benefits and in loss of management contributions.
Eighty-four years ago, in 1890, Canadian women were told they did not need the vote for they could accomplish as much by loving persuasion of their men. The argument failed to take into consideration the growing number, even at that time, of unmarried women wage earners who had no husbands to persuade, lovingly or otherwise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In 1974, women's pension plans are still based on the assumption that women employees are all supported by men who will provide well for all contingencies, and that women have no financial responsibilities for dependents and no need to plan for their own economic well-being or that of their dependents.
However, the fact of the matter is that over a quarter of a million working women, 266,000, or almost one-tenth, of the female working force, are separated, deserted, divorced or widowed. Add to these over a million single women, 1,006,000, who make up more than a third, in fact 34.1 per cent of the female labour force, and the assumption of no female employee need becomes hard to support.
In this day of early marriage, the fact that only one-third of the female labour force, 33.3 per cent, is under the age of 25 is also a meaningful statistic.
Another consideration which must not be overlooked concerns those women in the labour force who are married, and that is the level of earnings of the male breadwinner. Many women who work do so in order to maintain a decent standard of living which the husband's wage alone would not permit. Pensions are generally assessed on the basis of average earnings over a period of time. Where those average earnings are low, the earned pension will also be low. If the wife's earnings are needed to establish a healthy life-style for the family during her working years, her pension is also needed to allow the couple a decent standard of living when they retire, and income replacement is needed if she becomes unable to work because of illness.
Disability insurance for women is limited in availability, and higher premiums are charged to women than men, as much as 61 per cent higher. The annual premium differential is said to be based on actuarial tables. However, insurance companies are quite coy about releasing the data on which they base their discriminatory premium rates for disability insurance. This is particularly strange because they freely publish the life tables on which they base their justification for discriminating between men and women in connection with retirement pensions and annuities. Perhaps they fear being embarrassed by discovery that this discrimination is due to emotional bias and myth and cannot be supported by fact.
Statistics Canada labour force survey indicates that the pattern of absences from work because of illness for the last number of years has been fairly consistent. The rate of absences because of short-term illness is somewhat higher for women than for men, but the rate for long-term illness, and it is this type of illness for which disability insurance is made available, is higher for men than for women. In 1973, 1.82 per cent of all full-time working women were

absent from employment because of illness lasting for a period in excess of one week; during the same year 1.97 per cent of all full-time working men were absent because of illness lasting over one week.
Canadian suffragists at the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of this century were part of a more general reform movement that was concerned to remove a wide range of injustices and evils that afflicted the country at that time. Contemporary Canadian women, too, usually see women's rights in the broad context of human rights and social betterment.
Situations which are unfair to women are usually closed situations where some persons are able to make and implement decisions which they do not have to explain or account for and, therefore, are situations which are unfair to some men also, especially those from minority groups. Opening up situations for discussion and requiring reasons for decisions normally results in increased representation not only of women but of men from minority groups.
As long as discrimination against women in pension plans and life insurance continues, and insurance companies are not required to account fully for their practices, one must wonder what other forms of discrimination may be practised on the grounds of secret actuarial tables, and what the cost is to the economy as well as to the individuals concerned.
Human rights codes generally stress public education, and research into attitudinal change and cultural conditioning. But people who are discriminated against, whether on the grounds of sex, colour or race, are increasingly interested in changing behaviour rather than attitudes. Changing attitudes is a slow and nebulous business. Changing differential treatment in existing benefit schemes is much more susceptible to clear definition and practical solutions.
It is my hope that the human rights legislation which is due to come before this House will deal firmly and fairly with this matter. It is surely in the interest of the Canadian economy, as well as in the interest of justice, that there should be fairness and equity in every phase of employment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure you are well aware of the fact that it is with a surplus budget of some $250 million that this Liberal administration intends to carry out its operation which, by the way, has been rendered twice as difficult, when we considered the budget speech the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) made last Monday night, which aims at reducing the inflation rate and prevent the Canadian economy from entering into a long-lasting recession period.
If I remember correctly, in the first budget speech for the year 1974-75 which he made in May of this year, the minister had announced that he would fight inflation with a deficit budget of some $450 million.
November 25, 1974

In spite of this, Madam Speaker, I consider that he is not offering any valid solution to fight inflation, and that the measures proposed by the minister are clearly not enough for our people in the low-income bracket. At best, as far as I can judge, the minister is about to invite provincial governments to reduce their public expenses and incite Canadian workers and corporations to exert a minimum of discipline.
As the hon. Minister of Finance said: "Canada is confronted by two major challenges-dealing with persistent, deep-seated inflation and at the same time maintaining a good level of production and employment". I do not feel that the minister's budget speech can solve those two problems because, first of all, they are contrary and they require different solutions. The budget is only grappling with the effects of inflation while hoping the price increase for 1975 will be lower by about 1 per cent compared to the increase for this year.
But what about the causes, Madam Speaker? We keep claiming from all sides that this plague we call inflation is imported, but it does not seem that Ottawa has decided to come to grips with it. On the contrary, we find rather easily that some measures are clearly inflationist and that the said inflationary thrusts for 1975 come from inside.
While all great nations in the whole world are trying to innovate and find new ways to deal with this problem, Ottawa is at the same time doing its utmost to convince Canadian people that there is not much possibility to check inflation and that meanwhile we have to bear our pain patiently.
On the other hand, I am happy to see that Ottawa has finally understood-even though not entirely in my opinion, but it still is a first step towards understanding- considering that the federal government has decided to lower the sales tax on building materials from 12 to 5 per cent. However, I do not think that the government and its building speculator friends will suffer much, since the government used to keep this tax for itself and the big builders still increased their annual profits in unimaginable proportions.
Madam Speaker, in this budget which applies exceptionally to an eighteen month period rather than a normal year, it is surprising and even disappointing to note that Ottawa has not considered lowering the old age pensions admissibility age to 60 over a period of five years, in view of the fact that the government of the Prime Minister talked a lot about senior citizens during the last election campaign.
Moreover, the budget contains nothing to get agriculture out of its present stagnant situation, and according to the predictions of the hon. Minister of Finance, there will be in fact an increase in unemployment in the next few months, a decrease in production before the end of the year, and a rate of inflation of about 10 per cent in 1975.
Madam Speaker, I believe that it is not by granting income tax deductions of about $650 million for 1974 that the government can support the demand of the Canadian people and maintain at the same time Canadian production. This will only reduce somewhat the burden of Canadian taxpayers. In other words, the only true measure implemented by Ottawa to maintain the rate of
The Budget-Mr. Allard
growth of our economy consists in reducing the taxes for manufacturing industries and small companies, as well as mining and oil industries, which measure aims at increasing the offer and preventing shortages.
Madam Speaker, there is a very simple and well known way to shirk one's duty and present commitments and to forget current problems. It consists in trying to make predictions, in talking, in discussing, in argumenting about future problems. One thus seems knowledgeable, worried and concerned, while on the whole washing one's hands of problems that should be solved today.
Being unable to face the present wisely, coldly and objectively, one withdraws into the past, dreams about or fears the future. And problems take roots, remain and develop mostly because those responsible for solutions are caught in the machinery of conditioning or routine, following the well beaten path of their predecessors. However, Madam Speaker, the present requires an administration that can no longer follow patterns of the past. As can be seen we are courting disaster. Time has come for the federal government to make sure it takes the required steps to give all Canadians the purchasing power they need to do credit to Canadian production, thus spurring demand.
Several times, government members voted against proposals calling for the implementation of a guaranteed minimum income, which would allow each and every Canadian to live decently, according to the Canadian productive potential. Yet, I read in Le Devoir of November 21, 1974, that in about a year Canada could equip itself with a new federal-provincial guaranteed income system.
We, of the Social Credit, will not hesitate to apply such measures, because families must be assured of a decent income. We have been advocating the solution for years.
According to the rules and traditions of times past, and of the wonderful progressive capitalism of those past few decades in Europe and North America, the budget speech that was read out last Monday by the hon. Minister of Finance is undoubtedly a masterpiece of accuracy, status quo and stability of the present situation which protracts for a few months the very same problems of inflation, unemployment and poverty, without the flimsiest hope for national economic balance which every citizen in Canada has been expecting from our government.
And yet I shall accuse no one for their reluctance or even their carelessness. I find, Madam Speaker, that the officials at the head of most departments are doing everything they can. They are not to be blamed nor replaced they should simply be asked to alter their consistently retrospective mental attitude, their frame of thinking, and direct it to the present, which would benefit each and everyone of us, as soon as we would become conscious of our present capabilities.
If we go rapidly over our national economy since 1934, when the Bank of Canada was created, as a result of far reaching royal inquiries into our financial situation, our industry, our trade and banking system, we realize the huge progress made in every respect with the production and capitalization of huge supplies in the hands of prosperous citizens and great corporations private or public, millionaire or billionaire, national or multinational.
28543-36%

The Budget-Mr. Gillies
Production and capitalization have been in constant progress as opposed to the constant slowdown of consumption. If we admit that broad fact far and wide, Madam Speaker, then solutions will immediately arise which we shall behold with astonishment. We will just have to apply them easily and plainly in our usual work, in Parliament, without having to change people or monetary, economic or political systems.
All the monetary, economic and political systems and mechanisms which were used to build up a fantastic production and an extravagant surplus capitalization may well be used at the same time to regulate a more complete system of personal, family and social consumption under the leadership of the same ministers and members of Parliament elected last July 8 by the people of Canada who produce, consume and capitalize. We merely have to change a few percentage points in incomes and taxes between different places without harming anyone and by doing so much good to all with concrete results in both the national and world mentality almost desperately seeking a better economic national and world balance, and we can assure better distribution for all we can produce.
Madam Speaker, having reached a point where in 1974 we are boarding for the future as much as 42 per cent of our annual production and consuming the other 58 per cent, judging by the budget that is before us, where we Canadians are consuming in 1974 only $80 billion out of a production of $139 billion, thus capitalizing $59 billion for the future, I can clearly see, madam Speaker, that we should immediately transfer $15 billion of our exaggerated capitalization to make for the deficiency in our consumption. This would at once reduce or drive out inflation, unemployment and poverty and effect an immediate return to a national economic balance between individuals, families and companies in all parts of Canada, to start with, and this condition would soon spread to all parts of the world following our convincing experience.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the budget presented in this House a week ago tonight by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) dealt with three problems-inflation, unemployment and leadership. While it is true that these are the three problems faced by all Canadians, I suspect that they have a meaning for Canadians that is somewhat different from the meaning they have for the Minister of Finance.
The impact of inflation on the average Canadian today gives rise to a real fear about his ability to be able to cope with the rapidly increasing cost of living, indeed his ability to obtain even the basic necessities of life. I suspect that the impact of inflation on the Minister of Finance does not appear to concern his standard of living, though it may have some relationship to his advancement within the political spectrum.
The fear created by unemployment for the average Canadian is again the fear of the economic consequences of his loss of income. I expect that the fear created by unemployment for the Minister of Finance is the fear that if there is massive unemployment across Canada he will

not be employed in the position that he would like to have in the not too distant future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance talks about leadership, the leadership that he has in mind is different from the leadership that Canadians had hoped would be given them in the budget that came down recently. Otherwise, why would we have had this budget? I suggest we would have had a totally different budget from the minister.
Actually the budget brought down last Monday was a particularly irresponsible one in light of the international situation within which it was introduced. Every member of this House knows that we are probably facing and living in the most unsettled economic climate we have experienced for over a quarter of a century. From the end of world war II until 1972 the United States was willing to finance measures to meet international problems around the world. Today it cannot do this. The fact that it is no longer able to do so has been exacerbated by the fact that there has been an increase in the price of oil of over 400 per cent in the past year, creating an economic situation that is almost insoluble.
We in the industrial countries of the world have to find a way to settle a $40 billion balance of payments problem and to recycle $60 billion worth of petro dollars, and this still in the first year of this new situation. There is absolutely no way in which the existing central banking system and international monetary program can handle this particular problem. And here we have the Minister of Finance bringing down a budget that offers no solutions to these problems, and that makes no suggestion as to what Canada can do to alleviate the situation.
As Dr. Henry Kissinger, Secretary of State for the United States, said in Chicago on November 14, "collaboration among the industrialized countries of the world will be an inescapable necessity". The first part of this co-operation must be to bring down the rate of domestic inflation. In this era of economic tension and uncertainty, it seems to me almost inconceivable that the Minister of Finance would bring down one of the most divisive budgets ever brought down in the history of Canada. Why at this time, when we are teetering on the edge of international problems the like of which we have never before seen, would the Minister of Finance decide this is a good time for the federal government to interfere unilaterally with constitutional powers that were settled years and years ago?
What can be the thinking of the government in this regard? The federal government does not need the money; it has been collecting more money than it knows how to spend intelligently. Perhaps the government did this because it believes fundamentally in the centralization of authority in Ottawa, thus going against the trend to decentralization that most countries of the world think is the right one. It may be-though I would hate to credit this to the party opposite-that the government believes that for purely political purposes it benefits much more from confrontation than it does from conciliation. If this is the reason, Madam Speaker, what a dreadful situation in which to place the people of Canada at the present time.

I do not believe that the party opposite is quite as Machiavellian as that, though it is possible that it is, Madam Speaker. I think the reason the budget was brought down at this time, and the reason for this confrontation with the provinces constituted an attempt to try to divert attention from the way in which the government has been managing the economy in the last couple of years. What other reason is there for a budget of the sort we have at the present time?
The fact is that the Minister of Finance has brought down four budgets. Every single one of these budgets started out in the same way. They stated that the nation was facing unemployment and inflation, and through the process of all these four budgets no progress whatsoever has been made to deal with those twin problems. It seems to me that the terrifying thing about this budget is that the minister shows no comprehension of why we have unemployment at the present time.
The reason for unemployment in this country today is simply that the government has done nothing about inflation for the last couple of years. All of the forces bringing about unemployment today result from inflation. For example, look at the decline in housing starts, which show a 25 per cent drop. This rate will probably go higher. Why have we had this drop in housing starts? It was simply because of the interest rate policy that the government was following, a policy designed to do something to curb inflation but which just did not work.
Why are retail sales down 3 per cent? If these policies of the Trudeau government are continued Mr. Bennett will look like one of the most enlightened men of all times. Retail sales were down 3 per cent in the month of September because in spite of what the government says its policies are not keeping up the real standard of living of most Canadians.
Why do we have a decline in sales of manufactured products? I suggest it is partially because of a slowdown in other economies. However, the major reason is that we have become one of the highest cost producers in the world, with no increase in productivity but with an increase in cost and an increase in unemployment.
Why do we have the unenviable record of having more days lost through strikes and industrial unrest than any other industrial country in the world? I suggest the reason is because we have done nothing about inflation, and people have to use this device to try to maintain their standard of living high. We are in the middle of declining economic activity because of the inability of the government to do anything about the inflationary process, and in the middle of that situation what is so frightening is to have a budget that obviously does not perceive this as the major problem of the country at the present time.
The Minister of Finance forecast at the start of the year that we would have an increase in gross national product of 5 per cent. Some six months later it was 4 per cent-in six months time a decline of 20 per cent. There was little economic growth in the third quarter of this year and we will probably have none in the fourth quarter, and that is all because of the policies followed by the government. The one thing that was clear during the last parliament,
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
and is now clear during this parliament so far is that the foundation stone on which the Minister of Finance has built his policies to fight inflation has crumbled.
The way in which the Liberal government said it was going to fight inflation was by increasing supply, but where is that increased supply? Our gross national product is down, there is no increase in supply, and this policy of the government has been a total failure. That sort of a solution cannot work. The last person who tried this particular policy was Lyndon Johnson in the United States. He argued in the United States that they could have both guns and butter. I suggest you cannot have both-you cannot have both in this country just as they could not have both in the United States. You cannot expect the government and the private sector combined to take more out of the economy than the economy is producing, and if you try to do so you will end up with nothing but inflation, and that is precisely what we have today.
To say that after a year in which you have a 25 per cent or 30 per cent increase in government expenditure, in the midst of double-digit inflation, that you have really accomplished something, the next year by bringing expenditure down 15 per cent is simply nonsense, because that policy simply will not work. That policy is doomed to failure. It is a real disaster to have a Minister of Finance who came in with a budget a week ago saying that he is trying to cure the economic sicknesses in this country by giving it more of the same medicine-more government expenditure. That simply will not work.
The Minister of Finance and his government are talking now about a budgetary deficit for next year. I suggest that this will produce more inflation. The Minister of Finance obviously does not understand the problems under which the economy is operating at the present time. If there was ever such a thing as a tradeoff between inflation and unemployment, it is quite clear that does not exist now. We have both at the present time, and it is quite clear that the government's policies are not working. To think that you can deal with the unemployment problem in that way is obviously a great mistake.
The Minister of Finance must understand these things and the problems we are faced with, but the great question is why does he not do something about it? The only reason I can think of why the government and the Minister of Finance are not moving strongly is that they are afraid to provide the leadership necessary to deal with the problems. It is absolutely essential that we do have leadership now, but the Minister of Finance will not give it. He will not give it because it would be really unpopular, and no government and no politician ever made any yards fighting inflation. This is a very unhappy thing to have to do today, but let me tell you that if we cannot find people in this democratic system with sufficient courage to deal with these problems, we will have a very difficult time keeping our democratic institution viable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
History repeats itself, and it is very clear that if you do not control inflation, or at least keep inflationary expectations down, there is no way you can maintain a prosperous economy. If you cannot maintain a prosperous economy, then you cannot maintain a demo-

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
cratic institution. We had an over 10 per cent inflation rate last year, we have an over 10 per cent inflation rate this year, and the way things are going we will have even more next year. That is no way to maintain the fabric of our society. If we are not willing to use our democratic institutions to fight inflation then we are indeed in terrible trouble.
The Minister of Einance says that this is all an international problem. That has to be the greatest cop-out that has ever taken place in this House of Commons. How can anybody suggest that our inflation is all the result of an international problem? Can anybody really believe that the drop in housing starts and the increase in unemployment are the result of something that has happened in Spain or Portugal? Does anybody really believe that the decline in retail sales is the result of something that has happened someplace else in the world? Can anyone believe that the inflation we have here is the result of anything but the policies that we are following in this country?
I find it really quite astonishing that the Minister of Finance, who prides himself on travelling all around the world talking to other ministers of finance, would not take a look at the budgets other countries are bringing down. Regardless of where you look or of what ideology is involved, whether it be a socialist government such as that in England, a capitalist society such as that in Japan, or a society such as that in the United States, you do not find them following the policies advocated by this government. There is not a chancellor of an exchequer or a minister of finance who has brought down a budget recently that has not told the people that they will really have to work to solve the inflationary problems.
In this country, which has an inflationary rate of over 10 Vi per cent, we do not have to absorb any of the impacts of the increase in world oil costs with which other countries have to contend. With that sort of situation, the problems with which we are now faced seem to me to be unacceptable. I really believe that had the present Minister of Finance been a father of confederation there likely would never have been a birth, but there certainly would have been a lot of heavy breathing.
The fact is that we will not solve inflation unless we are ready to go after it with strong measures. Some people may feel that the situation we face in this country is not particularly serious. I suggest that it is very serious, and we will not long have the things that keep a private entreprise system going with a continuing rate of 10 per cent or 12 per cent inflation. We are going to require something far less, perhaps an inflation rate of 5 per cent, 6 per cent or 7 per cent.
Let us consider the record of Germany. It has an inflation rate of 6.8 per cent and a 3 per cent rate of unemployment, but that country is worried. If the Minister of Finance wants to make comparisons with other countries around the world he ought to be making comparisons with the OPEC countries at the present time.
Since I have been in this House of Commons I have tried to analyse what is taking place in our economy in terms of budgetary expenditure, tax and monetary policy, and I wonder why in a great country like Canada we cannot use our resources more effectively. I wonder why we have
anything like the inflation we have today. We have so many resources, and an agricultural community that is strong and productive. I can only conclude that while we have two real problems in this country, unemployment and inflation, the greatest economic problem we have is the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the budget debate. The budget speech, somewhat like the speech from the throne, brings the new member face to face, and rather brutally, with his role as a newly elected representative of the people.
I should like to attempt to be as faithful as possible a spokesman for the concerns of the constituents of Portneuf. Still, as it is always very difficult to speak on behalf of another person, I wonder if it is possible to speak for over 80,000 constituents, that is the population of the riding of Portneuf.
Be that as it may, I have tried to regroup as best I can my own reflections on what the electors pointed out to me during the few weeks of the election campaign, as well as on the comments I heard during my numerous meetings with various groups in my riding since the election on July 8.
I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, how much I respect my constituents and my predecessor in this House, Mr. Godin. I take this opportunity to announce to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all hon. members, that Mr. Godin has been elected alderman of an industrial town in Portneuf riding, called Donnacona. I want to congratulate him and wish him every success in his new duties.
Portneuf is a beautiful and large riding, a third of which is a rural community and two thirds are highly urbanized. I am very happy to find that the measures announced in the budget speech will affect all groups of these citizens.
The first point that holds my attention in this budget speech has to do with housing. From all corners of Portneuf riding, my constituents will benefit from these measures. The urban area is in full development in terms of low cost and average cost of private residences.
The reduction to 5 per cent of the sales tax on building materials, plus the $500 subsidy will make it possible to save approximately $1,100 on the purchase of a new house.
The registered home ownership savings plan will certainly help a large number of young people in my constituency who had hardly any hope of becoming home owners.
These measures plus the elimination of sales tax on municipal transit systems and water distribution equipments will certainly improve the lot of municipalities.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give some indications of the way these measures will favour the voters of the Portneuf riding.
The first group concerned will be affected in an indirect way. In both the Eastern and Western ends of my constituency, there are a number of saw-mills as well as producers of building materials of various types, including insulation panels, acoustic tiles, bricks and cement blocks.

November 25, 1974

It is obvious that the renewal of activities in the construction of new housing will be an incentive for those firms and clear the unemployment threat which haunted the numerous employees in this industry.
In the urban part of my riding, we will also witness a renewal in the construction sector. In addition to provide many jobs to the workers in this sector, that renewal will favour home ownership and better housing.
Many young people, in particular, will avail themselves of the new Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, and the day will come faster for them to become owner of their own house. Whether in Riviere-a-Pierre, in Saint-Raymond, in Pont-Rouge, in the district of Les Saules or in Loretteville, many citizens will take advantage of those measures announced in the budget speech, measures dealing with housing policy.
Still in that field, it seems to me that we should take steps so that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is our national housing corporation, upgrade its clauses for the protection of the new house buyer.
In the Des Saules district, for instance, numerous buyers have been wronged as a result of the financial difficulties of some builders. This situation should be provided for, mechanisms should be set up to protect the consumer. As an example, there could be an insurance plan under which an owner, as soon as he takes possession of his house, would deal directly with the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, so that he could complain and recriminate if there is anything wrong with the house.
It also happens that in those circumstances the sub-contractors suffer losses. We should change the terms under which loans are granted so that sub-contractors are assured of payment for work they have done on a particular house.
Agriculture is the second matter I should like to deal with. A large part of my riding of Portneuf consists of beautiful farm lands and many farmers are engaged in either dairy production, horticulture, or cattle breeding. All members have heard either through the media or during the special debate we had in the House, about the situation of farm producers in the province of Quebec.
During the election campaign, as well as since July 8, I have had the opportunity of discussing matters with many farmers in my riding. Today, being a farmer is really running a business. Investments are considerable, labour is hard to find, salaries are very high, and production costs vary from one season to another. As for the farmer, his income is subjected to the vagaries of very volatile markets. Which brings us to the problems such as the one we witnessed in Quebec with regard to certain grades of beef cattle sent to the slaughterhouse.
The media show us regularly cases of people who suffer from starvation or malnutrition throughout the world. In the meantime, the owners of beautiful farms, real gardens, whether it be at Neuville, at Cap-Sante or elsewhere, are thinking of quitting the land because they can no longer cope with the job, because their children do not want to take a gamble in a field they consider much too uncertain. Mr. Speaker, we must get our agriculture out of its insecurity, we must support our minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) when he is brought face to face with the
The Budget-Mr. Bussieres
disparagers of marketing boards and other measures aimed at stabilizing the income of farm producers.
The tax reduction for small wage-earners contained in the budget will also be helpful to most of my constituents of Portneuf. They will thus recover the purchasing power which they had lost due to price increases. This provision as well as the possibility of deducting the first $1,000 of interest income will be beneficial to the budgets of Canadian taxpayers.
The constituents of Portneuf are aware that inflation means profits for some people. They realize that it helps increase government revenue but they are pleased to see that the minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has given up a certain amount of revenue to help them make both ends meet. The budgetary measures are correcting the situation and the government is in a way refunding this inflationary revenue.
They are also aware that inflation benefits certain companies. And I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the last letter I received on that subject came from a businessman of Ancienne-Lorette. He pointed out that fact to me and stated his interest in a legislation that would provide a ceiling for profits or that would control company profiteering. This businessman's concern is the same as that of most of the people of Portneuf. They are anxious to see the minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) introduce legislation in this respect and they are assured that the minister is highly qualified to administer such a legislation in the best interest of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, if some companies lack social conscience to the point of using inflation to expand their profits in an exaggerated way, it is the duty of this government to take action and bring them to reason.
The constituency of Portneuf is also proud, Mr. Speaker, of having within its limits one of the most beautiful, the most modern and the biggest Canadian Forces base, the Valcartier base. The action of Canadian servicemen and their efficiency as peacekeepers is known throughout the world. Our servicemen are peace professionals. This may sound contradictory, but it is a contradiction that an old saying has recognized from time immemorial.
We used to hear when we were young, "If you want peace prepare for war". For us, Canadians, the need or even the usefulness of armed forces is not so obvious. Public opinion is strongly divided in that respect, and government decisions must take into account Canadian public opinion. However, we must not for that matter lose sight of the need to increasingly qualify the staff of our armed forces and provide them with the best equipment available to ensure quality of service and also guarantee the viability of this career they chose to enter. Young people are still being recruited. Those young people must feel that they are entering an open road into the future and not a dead end street that would make them regret their decision after a few years. Last summer, Mr. Speaker, an unfortunate accident occurred at the Valcartier base. This accident is much more regrettable because it has stricken young cadets in training. Some quarters have taken this opportunity to make a quick trial to the Armed Forces and the cadets corps. However, I want to express my appreciation to the cadet corps. I also want to express

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Bussieres
it to the militia groups who devoted their time and experience to the training of young cadets.
When I was a student I had the opportunity to belong to a cadet corps for five years. I highly appreciated the qualities of discipline and other aspects of the manly education that is given there. These days, when everything encourages free-and-easiness and inaction, when more and more people are asking themselves questions on the quality of discipline in our schools, we should increase our efforts in favour of the renewal of these cadet corps.
I would also like to mention that the many people who work at the Valcartier military base have great difficulty with highway traffic. It must also be mentioned that Ville Belair is the place where all military and civilian personnel pass through on their way to Camp Valcartier. The citizens of this residential community are gradually being chocked up by a volume of traffic that is becoming quite a hindrance. The Citizens' Committee who favours the expansion of Henri IV Blvd. should get all our attention.
The leather industry is another interesting sector in the industry of Portneuf riding. Whether in Saint-Emile, the Huron Village in Loretteville or l'Ancienne Lorette, there are many manufacturers of moccassins, shoes, slippers and gloves. This industry uses very qualified local manpower and in spite of fleeting difficulties, the management of these establishments show dynamism and imagination in improving the quality of their products and finding new markets for them. However, there is always a menace hovering over this type of business and that is meeting import competition. These manufacturers are counting on the clearsightedness of the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) to help their products keep their place on our markets and thus keep employment high in places where unemployment is a sore that too often must be patched up.
I would find myself wanting if, in conclusion, I did not point out the interest shown by the citizens of Portneuf riding for the budget of May last. That budget quickly became one of the main topics for discussion during the election campaign. I must also add that there has been some apprehension since the election of last July 8. Some doubts were being shown about the new budget as it was feared that the majority government might go back on the good intentions that were set out in last May's budget. I am pleased that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) kept the same approach, making it possible for the Canadian people to breathe better in spite of the suffocating atmosphere around the world economy.
Some hon. members reproached the government for having thrown all the blame for the present state of our economy on the situation in other countries. Others said the measures were good but came in too late.
Mr. Speaker, the budget of the hon. Minister of Finance is marked with carefulness, not the carefulness of the pusillanimous but of the realistic, the carefulness of a government which is open to the world, which knows the volume of its exports and imports and does not want to retire within itself.
As to those who think the measures are good but come in too late, they will be the first, Mr. Speaker, to claim that

the government acted this way because of them. They will be the first to boast that they recommended these measures and that the government listened to them at last. But they will make these remarks when it brings them political dividends.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate again the Minister of Finance for the interest expressed in his budget speech towards everything which is of concern to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now in another budget debate, another budget which is really failing to deal with inflation, another budget out of a shotgun with shotgun measures trying to deal with inflation. In the few minutes I have I should like to deal with some of the shortcomings in the budget.
Any provisions to provide aid for farmers are noticeably absent from the budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was no further mention of incentives for farmers, including the stabilization of incomes and markets, as promised in the Speech from the Throne. It would seem apparent that to curb inflation and relieve the international food crisis the Canadian farmer requires massive assistance to expand his production to meet Canadian and world needs. This assistance could have been made available by special interest rates and relaxed loan conditions on the farm improvement loans plan; easier financing for clearing unused arable land; the upgrading of existing land and investments in machinery, agrichemicals and modern techniques; and government investment in research development assistance.
Indeed no effort was made to aid the agricultural sector through financial stimultation of co-operation between production and transportation toward alleviating the often critical distribution problem. I might say in this connection that the fruit industry in British Columbia is again having trouble with the transportation of its fruit.
One last remedy available to the government to cure the current inflation and hunger ills was financially to encourage Canadian farmers to adopt more efficient agricultural techniques to increase crop outputs. A generous new investment in agriculture would increase the potential of increased food surpluses, thereby satisfying one objective of the budget, that is, to increase supply and would also represent a step toward alleviating the world food and hunger crisis.
If the government were really sincere in its intent to combat inflation it would devise programs for using some of the money now being used for LIP programs and UIC benefits to construct canneries and granaries to take care of agriculture surpluses. Such a program would put a lot of unemployed to work, cutting down on high unemployment and on taxes required for UIC benefits and LIP programs.
The lack of any concrete programs to use agricultural surpluses to bolster our economy and decrease unemploy-
November 25, 1974

ment clearly indicates that the government is unable to identify with the critical areas within the Canadian economy; it is unable to initiate appropriate operative programs for effective relief.
For many Canadians the reduction in personal income tax will be welcome news, but Canadians will realize in due course that this reduction in their income tax is really, in fact, further depreciating the value of their spending dollar. As long as the cost of living prices remain as they are, these personal income tax reductions will benefit Canadians, but the budget does not get to the heart of attacking inflation or finding ways to curb it, and inflation and the cost of living will go up considerably in the months ahead.
Any benefits Canadians will receive because of the reduction in their personal income tax will soon be eroded by the increase in the cost of living and inflation. What the government has attempted to do is to lull Canadians into thinking it is being a big brother to them by reducing their personal income tax. Canadians will soon realize they have been duped when they find prices of their goods going up and their spending dollar being further reduced in value. Whatever benefits they are going to receive now will be taken away from them in due course, simply because the government has done nothing to check inflation and the increase in the cost of living.
In the budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) stated that he would hold the increase in government expenditures at 15 per cent next year, compared with the 24 per cent increase in the current year's expenditure over last year's. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) recently tabled in the House supplementary estimates totalling $25,951 million for the fiscal year 1974-75.
In a recent CTV interview the Minister of Finance stated that it was "intensely difficult in the political process to hold these expenditures down. You've got the legitimate ambitions of ministers of departments." It seems to me that some of those legitimate ambitions of ministers have greatly increased the financial burdens of the Canadian people. I am especially recalling the $510 million deficit in the UIC program, brought about by a previous minister's inability to manage his department properly. The ones who were forced to pay in the end for that deficit were the Canadian people.
It would seem to me that ministerial ambitions, especially at a time when we have high unemployment, inflation running rampant and the cost of living constantly going up, should rank second, and ministers should be finding ways to curb wasteful spending in their departments. They have an obligation to the Canadian people, who elected them to the positions they are now holding, to do so. There is no justification for the increase in government spending and waste when the people of this nation are experiencing high unemployment, increases in the cost of living, and depreciation of their spending dollar.
Any reduction or help in reducing the cost of homes is certainly welcome, but sales tax on building materials should be entirely abolished. The reduction to 5 per cent is a step in the right direction, but the government should
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
have totally abolished the sales tax. The 5 per cent sales tax will leave intact the existing bureaucracy for collecting the building material tax; it will be just as complicated a set-up as the one which collected the 11 per cent tax. Another bureaucracy must now be set up to administer the new program under which each purchaser of a new home is to get $500. If this is a key to the job creation program which this government has in mind for next year, it's a great way of fighting inflation.
Under the present set-up we are not providing an incentive for young Canadian families who want to build and own a home. Our present structure alienates young people from building and owning a home. They find building, costs, land costs, etcetera, more than they can handle. If we completely abolish the sales tax on building materials, the bureaucracy created for collecting the sales tax can be eliminated and materials would be available at prices most Canadians could afford. The long-term effect of this would be a substantial decrease in our housing shortage.
News of benefits granted to our old age pensioners is welcome; but if in the months ahead these benefits are to be swallowed up by the spiralling rate of inflation and increase in the cost of living, our pensioners will be no further ahead. Pensioners fortunate enough to receive an income from a registered savings plan or from a deferred profit-sharing plan will much appreciate the exemptions provided for those. Pensioners with $30,000 invested and old age pension supplements do not now pay any tax, or very little, so that many of the proposed new benefits will apply only to those fortunate enough to be in higher income brackets.
For those pensioners who are not so fortunate, who are only receiving old age security, the news is not so good. The budget has failed to provide them with added protection against inflation and increases in the cost of living. Single pensioners who are receiving only the basic minimum of about $2,700 will feel the ravages of inflation and increases in the cost of living. Present conditions make it almost impossible for them to enjoy a decent existence. The government has failed those pensioners whose only source of income is their old age security pension, because it has not provided for any pension increases. The government must stop dishing out piecemeal benefits to these hard-pressed pensioners. The government has an obligation to provide this segment of our population with adequate protection in order that these people can cope effectively with inflation and the high cost of living which is constantly eroding the purchasing power of their pensions. Something more substantial must be done for pensioners who are receiving only the old age security pension. This budget has done nothing for them. It has left them more vulnerable to the further ravages of inflation and increases in the cost of living.
The government proposals in the budget to provide incentives for incorporated small businesses by increasing the annual limit on profits taxed at the 25 per cent special rate to $100,000 from $50,000, and the cumulative limit to $500,000 from $400,000 may benefit our small business owners, although I do not think the benefits are substantial enough to encourage more Canadians to own small businesses. These incentives, however, will enable some to capitalize on their expansion.

November 25, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
The Liberal government has never seemed to realize that the backbone of the economy of this nation centres on small business. Small businesses account for over 50 per cent of Canada's gross national product, and they pay 50 per cent of the taxes collected by the government.
The small business is also the breeding ground for new industries. What may be a small business today can become a leading industry tomorrow. Unfortunately, the government does not see it this way, and as other segments of our country receive more and more benefits the small business segment of our population receives less and less. The government's policies on small business have been such that many have been allowed to go into bankruptcy because they have not been provided with adequate financial means or incentives to enable them to survive and compete.
The government is willing to make substantial loans to foreign governments for the benefit of the relatively large corporations in Canada, but when it comes to making loans available to small Canadian businesses from Canadian banks, it turns a deaf ear. The budget incentives for small businesses in Canada are not good enough.
It is time the government took its head out of the sand and took a good look at the present system which favours foreign-owned companies over Canadian owned companies which for years have formed the backbone of the economy of this country.
There are a few really depressed areas in my constituency of Okanagan-Boundary. One is the beef industry. The ranchers in the area pioneered this country. They were one of the backbones of the economy. Because of the policies of the government they are in one of the worst situations they have ever faced in history.
There is a large lumber industry in British Columbia. Today it is very hard pressed. I realize that as far as this government is concerned, a lot of the input into the lumber industry comes from the provincial government. However, the federal government still has an obligation toward this industry.
There is an extensive mining industry in my constituency. This industry has also been a pioneer in my constituency. It has been going on for many, many years. However, the way the industry is being treated by governments today, it will not be around much longer. It is well-known that there should be more exploration. More mines could be in the area. It was only a few short years ago that one of the leading copper mines was discovered and developed. With this kind of situation in those three leading industries, it will be very hard for the people in my area, and for Canadians in general.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
